(dated) In English common law, a person who accuses a confederate; one who commits approvement.
senses.example: In the old trial, the approver named his accomplices in exchange for leniency.
senses.label: dated

core.definition: A person who approves something or gives official consent to it.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the second syllable, PROO, and end with a weak American r-colored vowel. Keep it to two syllables after the stress; do not add an extra syllable at the end.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it describes a role or function without praise or blame.
nuance.usage_note: In American business, approver is used in workflow software and corporate settings: 'The approver receives the request first.' In everyday talk, people more often say 'the person who signs off' or 'the decision maker.' The older legal sense, from English common law, refers to an accomplice who accused others in return for a pardon; this is historical and rare in the US.

distinctions.note: A reviewer examines and comments on something; an approver has the authority to give final consent.
A sponsor supports or funds someone or something; an approver decides whether something is acceptable.

examples.everyday: My dad is the approver for our family's big purchases, so I have to ask him first.
examples.professional: Each change request needs a named approver before it can be merged into the main branch.
examples.analytical: In older English law, an approver was an accused person who turned against his accomplices in exchange for a pardon.

nuance.analogy: Like the gatekeeper with the official stamp: nothing passes until they say yes.
nuance.etymology: From approve plus the agent suffix -er.
common_mistakes: Confusing approver (the person) with approval (the act or permission).
Using approver in everyday speech when a plainer phrase like 'the person who signs off' sounds more natural.

senses.definition: Initialism of anti-suit injunction.
Initialism of artificial superintelligence.
Initialism of automatic semicolon insertion.

core.definition: Anti-suit injunction: a court order that stops a party from pursuing a lawsuit in another court or country.

pronunciation.tip: Americans say each letter separately, with the strongest stress on the final I, which sounds like eye. Do not run the letters together as one word, like ASS-ee or AH-see.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it is a technical legal term with no emotional charge, although seeking one can signal a hostile dispute.
nuance.usage_note: In American legal and business circles, ASI is spoken as three letters, and lawyers usually write out the full term at first mention. Outside law, ASI also means artificial superintelligence in AI discussions and automatic semicolon insertion in JavaScript, so check the context and ask which meaning is intended in a meeting.

distinctions.note: The same letters name a different concept in AI; there, ASI means an AI that surpasses human intelligence across all areas.
Artificial general intelligence refers to human-level capability across tasks, while ASI in AI discussions refers to intelligence beyond that level.

examples.everyday: My brother works in international law, and he was on the phone all night about some ASI.
examples.professional: Legal has drafted an ASI motion to halt the parallel case in London until our Delaware hearing is decided.
examples.analytical: An anti-suit injunction restrains a litigant from pursuing proceedings abroad, which raises difficult questions of comity between national courts.

nuance.analogy: Like a traffic officer telling a driver to stop taking a second road that leads to the same destination.
nuance.etymology: Initialism of anti-suit injunction; injunction comes from Latin injunctio, a command.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the letters as one word, like ASS-ee, instead of saying A-S-I.
Assuming ASI always means artificial superintelligence; in legal meetings it means anti-suit injunction.

senses.definition: A violent onset or attack with physical means, for example blows, weapons, etc.
senses.example: The army made an assault on the enemy.

senses.definition: A violent verbal attack, for example with insults, criticism, and the like.
senses.example: She launched a written assault on the opposition party.

senses.definition: An attempt to commit battery: a violent attempt, or willful effort with force or violence, to do hurt to another, but without necessarily touching the person, such as by raising a fist in a threatening manner, or by striking at the person and missing.
senses.example: He was charged with assault after raising his fist and threatening the man in the parking lot.

senses.definition: The crime whose action is such an attempt.
senses.example: She was convicted of assault and sentenced to two years of probation.

senses.definition: An act that causes someone to apprehend imminent bodily harm (such as brandishing a weapon).
senses.example: Waving the gun at the clerk was an assault, even though he never fired a shot.

senses.definition: The tort whose action is such an act.
senses.example: The lawsuit alleged assault and battery, arguing the bouncer's threat had caused her real fear.

senses.definition: A non-competitive combat between two fencers.
senses.example: The fencing instructor staged an assault between two students to demonstrate footwork.

senses.definition: To attack, physically or figuratively; to assail.
senses.example: Tom was accused of assaulting another man outside a nightclub.

senses.definition: To threaten or harass. (Can we add an example for this sense?)
senses.example: The gang began to assault the neighborhood's shop owners with constant threats and harassment.

core.definition: A violent physical attack on someone, or a sudden, forceful effort to overcome or attack something.

pronunciation.tip: The stress is on the second syllable, SAWLT, with a vowel like the one in 'caught'. The l is silent, so it sounds like 'sawt'. Learners often pronounce the l, which Americans do not.

nuance.connotation: Strongly negative. It describes violence or aggression, and in legal or news contexts it signals a crime.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use assault in police reports, news, and everyday talk about violent crimes. In American law, assault often means threatening or attempting to hit someone, while battery means actual physical contact, although many states combine the two as assault and battery. Figurative uses, such as a heavy assault of questions, are natural in casual talk.

distinctions.note: Attack is the general and everyday word, while assault is more forceful, often violent, and used more in legal or military contexts.
In US law, battery is the actual unlawful touching of another person, while assault is often the threat or attempt that may not involve contact.

examples.everyday: The news said a man was charged with assault after a fight outside the bar.
examples.professional: Our legal team reviewed the complaint, which described the incident as an assault and not a simple disagreement.
examples.analytical: The author argues that the modern attention economy is an assault on human focus, not just a set of distractions.

nuance.analogy: An assault is like a storm breaking over a house: sudden, forceful, and aimed at breaking through its defenses.
nuance.etymology: From Old French asaut, from Latin assaltus, past participle of assilire, to leap upon.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the l, as in uh-SAWL-t, which Americans do not.
Using assault for a mild verbal disagreement, which sounds too strong.
Confusing assault with battery, which in US law means physical contact.

assault.etymology: From Middle English *assaut*, from Old French noun *assaut*, derived from the past participle of the verb *assalir*, from Late Latin *assalio*, from Latin *ad* (“at, towards”) + *saliō* (“jump”).

senses.definition: One to whom a thing is assigned.
senses.example: The assignee received the copyright once the author signed the transfer document.

senses.definition: One to whom a right or property is being transferred.
One who is appointed to act or speak in place of another; an agent.
senses.example: The court appointed an assignee to manage the bankrupt company's remaining debts.

core.definition: A person or organization to whom a right, job or property is formally transferred or given.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the final NEE, so the first syllables are weak. Pronounce the final syllable as a long e, like the e in see.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it is a precise legal and business term.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use assignee mainly in legal, financial and business writing about leases, patents and contracts. In everyday speech they say the new owner or the person who took it over. It is a formal, neutral term that you will see on documents rather than hear in conversation.

distinctions.note: The assignor transfers the right; the assignee receives it.
A grantee receives property or rights by a formal grant, often from a government or trust; an assignee receives an existing right or contract by assignment.

examples.everyday: The landlord said I'd have to be the assignee on the lease if I want to take over the apartment.
examples.professional: Please add the new assignee to the contract, since legal has approved the transfer.
examples.analytical: The court's ruling depends on whether the assignee takes the rights subject to the same defenses that the assignor faced.

nuance.analogy: Like a new owner receiving the keys to a house, the assignee receives rights that someone else hands over.
nuance.etymology: From Anglo-French assigné, past participle of assigner, 'to assign'.
common_mistakes: Confusing assignee with assignor: the assignee receives, the assignor transfers.
Stressing the first syllable as AS-ih-nee; the main stress is on the last syllable.

assignee.etymology: From Middle English *assigne*, from Old French *assigné*, equivalent to *assign* + *ee*.

senses.definition: The act of associating.
senses.example: The association of the two brands in customers' minds boosted sales.

senses.definition: The state of being associated; a connection to or an affiliation with something.
Any relationship between two measured quantities that renders them statistically dependent (but not necessarily causal or a correlation).
senses.example: The association between smoking and lung disease was clear in the cohort data.

senses.definition: A group of persons associated for a common purpose; an organization; society.
senses.example: She joined a professional association of data scientists based in Chicago.

senses.definition: Relationship between classes of objects that allows one object instance to cause another to perform an action on its behalf.
senses.example: In object-oriented design, an association lets one class call methods on another.

core.definition: A link or connection between things, people, or ideas, or a group that people form for a shared purpose.

pronunciation.tip: The primary stress falls on the -AY- syllable, and the final -tion is a 'shun' sound. The 'ci' is pronounced like 'see,' not 'shee,' in this word.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It can describe a helpful link, a club, or a statistical relationship, and the context shows which sense is meant.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'association' for groups like homeowners associations, trade associations, and professional organizations. In everyday talk, people say 'in association with' when naming a partner, and 'word association' is a common game. In data and research settings, it means a statistical link, which is not the same as cause.

distinctions.note: Affiliation is a formal membership or official link to an organization. Association is broader and can be informal, as in a link between ideas.
In statistics, correlation is a specific measure of linear relationship. Association is a broader term for any dependence between variables.
Connection is a general word for any link. Association often describes a mental link, a group, or a statistical relationship.

examples.everyday: Our homeowners association is sending everyone a notice about the new parking rules.
examples.professional: The analysis found a strong association between late deployments and customer complaints, so we need to test whether one causes the other.
examples.analytical: Association in a statistical model does not imply causation, and a careful analyst must distinguish confounding from genuine mechanism.

nuance.analogy: An association is like two houses on the same street that show similar patterns: they are linked by location, but one does not cause the other.
nuance.etymology: From Latin 'associatio,' meaning 'a joining together,' from 'associare,' meaning 'to join to.'
common_mistakes: Treating a statistical association as proof of causation, which is a common error in data reports.
Using 'association' as a verb, when the verb is 'associate.' Say 'I associate that smell with home,' not 'I association that smell.'
Saying 'association with' and 'association of' interchangeably. Use 'association with' for links between two things.

senses.definition: Malapropism of at first blush.

core.definition: A common mishearing of 'at first blush'; it is not standard, and it means the same as 'on first impression.'

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on 'bluff,' which ends in an f sound. The correct idiom ends in 'blush,' with the sh sound, so listen for that difference.

nuance.connotation: Neutral, but using it in writing or formal speech makes the speaker look careless.
nuance.usage_note: 'At first bluff' is a malapropism, a mishearing and misuse of 'at first blush.' Americans would notice it as an error, though they would understand it in casual speech. In writing or in professional talk, use 'at first blush' instead; the examples below use the correct form.

distinctions.note: At first blush is the standard idiom meaning on first impression; at first bluff is a mistaken form with no separate meaning.
A bluff is a pretense or a steep cliff; it is a different word and does not share the idiom's meaning.

collocations: at first blush the plan looks
at first blush the idea sounds

examples.everyday: At first blush the new phone seems great, but the battery barely lasts a day.
examples.professional: At first blush the proposal looks expensive, but the maintenance savings are substantial.
examples.analytical: At first blush the argument appears circular, yet on closer reading it turns on a substantive premise about intent.

nuance.analogy: Mishearing 'blush' as 'bluff' is like misreading a word on a menu: the meaning is close but the word is wrong.
nuance.etymology: Bluff comes from Dutch or Low German roots meaning 'blunt' or 'broad'; the idiom it resembles is 'blush.'
common_mistakes: Writing 'at first bluff' in formal writing instead of 'at first blush.'
Pronouncing 'blush' with an f sound, which turns the idiom into 'bluff.'

senses.definition: The theory that all gross matter is composed of atoms.
senses.example: Dalton's atomic theory held that every element consists of identical, indivisible particles.

senses.definition: Any of several theories that explain the structure of the atom, and of subatomic particles.
senses.example: The physics professor explained how the Bohr model fits into modern atomic theory.

core.definition: The scientific idea that all matter is made of tiny indivisible particles called atoms.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the TAH in atomic and the THEE in theory. The word theory has a long e sound, not the short i of 'thin', and the first syllable of atomic is a weak uh.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a standard term in science education and history of science.
nuance.usage_note: American students learn atomic theory in high school chemistry, usually starting with John Dalton's model and moving to modern quantum models. In everyday talk Americans may say 'the atomic model' for a particular picture of atoms. The word theory here means a well-tested scientific explanation, not a guess.

distinctions.note: Atomism is a philosophical doctrine dating from ancient Greece, while atomic theory is the modern scientific account built on measurement and experiment.
An atomic model is a specific picture or representation of atomic structure, while atomic theory is the broader body of principles behind it.

examples.everyday: My daughter's chemistry homework is all about atomic theory, and honestly I can't remember much of it.
examples.professional: Our materials team checks the new simulation against atomic theory before we trust its results.
examples.analytical: Dalton's atomic theory changed chemistry by treating each element as having atoms of a characteristic mass, rather than as a continuous substance.

nuance.analogy: Atomic theory is like an ingredient list for a recipe: it says what the basic units are and how they combine, not what the finished dish looks like.
nuance.etymology: Atomic from Greek atomos 'indivisible'; theory from Greek theoria 'contemplation, speculation, viewing'.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing theory as THAIR-ee or with a short i sound, instead of THEE-uh-ree.
Thinking theory means a guess, when in science it means a well-tested explanation.
Saying atom theory in formal writing, when atomic theory is the standard term.

senses.definition: Pertaining to the dawn; dawning, eastern, like a new beginning.
senses.example: The poet praised the auroral hush that comes before a new day begins.

senses.definition: Rosy in color.
senses.example: Her cheeks had an auroral glow after the long walk in the cold.

senses.definition: Pertaining to the aurora borealis or aurora australis.
senses.example: Scientists at the observatory tracked auroral activity during the solar storm last week.

core.definition: Relating to the aurora, the northern or southern lights, or to the dawn in a poetic sense.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the second syllable, 'ROR'. The final syllable is a reduced 'uhl', so do not add an extra vowel. The 'r' is pronounced clearly in American English.

nuance.connotation: Neutral in scientific use; poetic and lovely in literary use.
nuance.usage_note: Americans most often encounter this word in astronomy or geography writing about the aurora borealis. In literary writing, it can refer to dawn. In everyday talk, you would more likely say 'northern lights' or 'the lights in the sky.'

distinctions.note: 'Aurora' is the noun for the lights or the dawn itself, while 'auroral' is the adjective describing something related to them.
'Polar' describes the regions near the poles, while 'auroral' describes the lights or events that appear there.

examples.everyday: We drove up to Alaska hoping to see the auroral lights over the lake.
examples.professional: The satellite is tracking auroral activity, so the communications team should expect some signal interference.
examples.analytical: The poet used auroral imagery to suggest a new beginning, linking the dawn to the promise of renewal.

nuance.analogy: An auroral sky is like a stage curtain of light, shifting and glowing before the show begins.
nuance.etymology: From Latin 'aurora', dawn, with the adjective ending '-al'.
common_mistakes: Confusing 'auroral' with 'aural', which means related to hearing.
Using 'auroral' in everyday speech where 'northern lights' is the common American phrase.

senses.definition: In an authentic manner; genuinely.
senses.example: The restaurant serves tacos authentically prepared, using the same recipes from her grandmother's village.

core.definition: In a genuine, real way; true to its origin, its nature or who someone really is, rather than fake or imitated.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the second syllable: aw-THEN. The i in the middle is short, like 'ih', and the ending is -ik-lee, not -ic-al-ly with extra syllables.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It praises something as real, original or sincere, though it can sound like marketing when overused.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use it in food, music, art and personal conversation: 'These tamales taste authentically Mexican.' It is also common in ads and self-help talk, where it can sound overused. A natural reply is 'That sounds great' or 'I'll have to try it.'

distinctions.note: Genuinely stresses sincerity of feeling or intent; authentically stresses real origin or faithfulness to a source.
Truly is broad and everyday; authentically is more specific about being an original, real version of something.

examples.everyday: The tacos at that food truck taste authentically Mexican, not like the usual Tex-Mex stuff.
examples.professional: Our product page should show the real mentors authentically, with photos from their actual work instead of stock images.
examples.analytical: Kierkegaard argues that a person can exist authentically only by choosing their own commitments rather than conforming to the crowd.

nuance.analogy: Like a handmade quilt compared with a machine-printed copy of its pattern: the same design, but only one came from the original hands.
nuance.etymology: From authentic, from Latin authenticus, from Greek authentikos 'original, genuine'.
common_mistakes: Stressing the first syllable, as in AW-then-tick-lee; the stress belongs on THEN.
Adding an extra syllable, saying aw-THEN-tik-AL-lee; the ending is simply -ik-lee.

senses.definition: Acting or occurring involuntarily, without conscious control.
Pertaining to the autonomic nervous system.

core.definition: Happening automatically without conscious control, such as breathing, heartbeat, or digestion; relating to the nervous system that controls these functions.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the third syllable, NOM, so don't say AW-tuh-nom-ic. Keep the first vowel as a clear 'aw' and the middle syllable reduced to 'tuh'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a clinical or scientific term, so it sounds precise rather than emotional.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this word mostly in medicine, biology, and health contexts, such as 'the autonomic nervous system.' In everyday talk people say 'automatic' or 'involuntary' instead. Saying 'autonomic' at a doctor's office or in a science meeting sounds natural and precise.

distinctions.note: Automatic is the everyday word for something that happens or runs without thought. Autonomic is the precise physiological term for body functions controlled by the autonomic nervous system.
Involuntary is a broader, everyday word for any action you do not decide to do. Autonomic specifically refers to the body's self-regulating nervous system.

examples.everyday: Don't worry about your heartbeat; it's autonomic, so your body handles it without you thinking about it.
examples.professional: The wearable sensor tracks autonomic responses like heart rate variability and skin conductance during the study.
examples.analytical: Descartes struggled to explain why involuntary processes like breathing and digestion seemed to escape the control of the will.

nuance.analogy: Like a building's thermostat and furnace running in the background, the autonomic system keeps the body's temperature and rhythm steady without anyone pressing a button.
nuance.etymology: From Greek autonomos, 'having its own laws,' combined with the adjective suffix -ic; the name was coined for the self-regulating nervous system in the 19th century.
common_mistakes: Stressing the first syllable as AW-tuh-NAH-mik or the wrong syllable, which makes the word hard to recognize.
Confusing it with 'autonomous,' which describes independence or self-government rather than body functions.

senses.definition: Filled with awe.
senses.example: The awed students stared at the telescope as the planet came into focus.

senses.definition: Having or showing awe.
senses.example: She gave an awed whisper when she saw the Milky Way from the mountain.

core.definition: Feeling great respect, admiration, or wonder toward something impressive, powerful, or beautiful.

pronunciation.tip: It is one syllable that rhymes with 'sawed'. The final d is voiced, so do not drop it to just 'aw'.

nuance.connotation: Positive; it describes respectful wonder and admiration.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'awed' to describe people who are impressed by something large or moving, such as a concert, a famous speaker, or a natural wonder. It often appears with 'by,' as in 'We were awed by the view.' A natural reply to 'I was awed by her speech' is 'Me too, it was incredible.'

distinctions.note: Amazed stresses surprise, while awed stresses respect and a sense of something greater than oneself.
Awestruck is stronger and more vivid, suggesting being overcome, while awed is milder.

examples.everyday: We were all awed by the fireworks over the lake last night.
examples.professional: The client was awed by the demo, so they asked us to scale it up for the spring launch.
examples.analytical: The psalmist, awed by the vastness of creation, turns from wonder to a question about human worth.

nuance.analogy: Being awed is like stepping into a cathedral and lowering your voice without being told to.
nuance.etymology: Awed is the past participle of awe, from Old Norse agi, meaning terror or dread.
common_mistakes: Using 'awed' with 'of' instead of 'by', as in 'awed of the view' instead of 'awed by the view'.
Confusing awed with 'awful', which means something very bad.

senses.definition: Any member of species of the genera Meles, Arctonyx, Mellivora or Taxidea, of mammals.
senses.example: A badger dug a burrow under the fence and vanished into the cornfield.

senses.definition: A native or resident of the American state, Wisconsin.
senses.example: Growing up in Madison, she always called herself a badger, even after moving to Chicago.

senses.definition: A person who is very fond of cricket.
senses.example: My British coworker is a badger who has watched every county match this season.

senses.definition: To pester; to annoy persistently; to press.
senses.example: He kept badgering her about her bad habits.

core.definition: To pester someone repeatedly until they agree to something or give in.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, and pronounce the middle sound as a 'j' sound, not a hard 'g'. The final -er is reduced and r-colored, so it is not 'BAD-ger' with a long a.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It suggests annoying, repeated pressure, though it can be used lightly among friends.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'badger' in everyday speech to describe someone who keeps pressing for an answer or action, as in 'Stop badgering me about dinner.' It often takes 'someone into doing something' or 'someone for something'. It is less harsh than harassment, but it can irritate the listener. A natural reply is 'Okay, I'll call them today, I promise.'

distinctions.note: Nag suggests repeated reminders or complaints about the same thing, while badger suggests persistent pressure to get a result.
Pester is milder and more casual, while badger implies more persistent, forceful pressing.
Harass is serious and can be illegal, while badger is informal and usually not a legal matter.

examples.everyday: My mom badgered me until I finally called my cousin back.
examples.professional: I don't want to badger the client, but we really need the signed contract by Friday.
examples.analytical: Reporters badgered the senator with pointed questions, hoping to expose a contradiction in his story.

nuance.analogy: Like a dripping faucet that keeps at you until you finally fix it.
common_mistakes: Using 'badger' for a single polite request; it describes repeated, persistent pressure.
Leaving out the object, as in 'He badgered until I agreed' instead of 'He badgered me until I agreed'.
Confusing the verb with the animal, which is a noun.

badger.etymology: From Middle English *bageard* (“marked by a badge”), from *bage* (“badge”), referring to the animal's badge-like white blaze, equivalent to *badge* + *-ard*.

senses.definition: In a baneful way.
senses.example: He spoke banefully about his rival, his voice dripping with quiet malice.

core.definition: In a harmful, destructive or poisonous way, often in a way that works quietly and does damage over time.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on BANE, the first syllable. The -ful ending is reduced to 'fuhl', not 'fool', and the final -ly is 'lee'. The IPA in the item, with 'fʊli' and a stressed second syllable, is not the standard American form.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It describes harm or destruction, often in a dark or sinister tone.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use banefully in speech. It appears in literary writing, sermons, and formal essays, usually to describe harm that works quietly. In everyday English, use harmfully, destructively, or poisonously instead.

distinctions.note: Harmfully is the plain, everyday word for causing damage, and it is the natural choice in most American contexts.
Destructively emphasizes the breaking or ruining of things, while banefully stresses a poisonous or quiet harm.
Perniciously describes harm that is gradual and hard to notice, and it is also a formal or literary word.

examples.professional: The memo warned that unchecked rumors were banefully undermining trust across the engineering team.
examples.analytical: Propaganda, the essay argues, works banefully by eroding the shared facts on which public reasoning depends.

nuance.analogy: Like poison slowly mixed into a well: the harm spreads quietly, and the water looks clear until the damage is done.
nuance.etymology: From 'bane' (Old English bana, slayer or destroyer), plus -ful and -ly.
common_mistakes: Confusing 'baneful' with 'banal', which means dull or ordinary.
Pronouncing the second syllable as 'fool', saying 'bane-FOOL-lee'.

senses.definition: One who conducts the business of banking; one who, individually, or as a member of a company, keeps an establishment for the deposit or loan of money, or for traffic in money, bills of exchange, etc.
senses.example: My cousin is a banker who approves small business loans in Ohio.

senses.definition: The dealer in a casino, or one who keeps the bank in a banking game.
senses.example: The banker flipped over the cards and the table erupted in cheers.

senses.definition: The stone bench on which a mason cuts or squares his work.
senses.example: The mason set the block on the banker and squared its edges carefully.

senses.definition: A type of envelope with a diamond shape or V-flap that opens on the long edge.
senses.example: She mailed the invitations in banker envelopes with V-shaped flaps.

senses.definition: A vessel employed in the cod fishery on the banks of Newfoundland.
senses.example: The old banker sailed from Gloucester each spring to fish the Grand Banks.

senses.definition: Synonym of browman.
A watercourse filled from bank to bank.
senses.example: After three days of rain, the river was a banker, filling its channel completely.

senses.definition: A bet that is almost certain to succeed.
senses.example: Betting on the favorite was a banker, the odds were so lopsided.

senses.definition: A very safe option.
senses.example: Sticking with the proven vendor felt like a banker for the procurement committee.

core.definition: A person who works in banking, especially a manager or owner of a bank or a financial institution.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable and do not pronounce the g. The final -er is a reduced, rhotic vowel, so say it as a soft 'ur' sound with a clear r.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It describes a profession, with some associations of wealth and power.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say 'banker' for a bank employee in management, finance, or investment, such as an investment banker. The everyday word for a bank employee who handles transactions at a counter is 'teller.' In card games like poker or blackjack, the dealer or the one holding the bank may also be called the banker.

distinctions.note: A teller handles routine cash and deposit transactions at a counter, while a banker usually has a management, lending, or advisory role.
A financier is a person who provides or manages large amounts of capital, which is a broader term than banker and can be used outside banks.

examples.everyday: My neighbor is a banker, so she always knows which loans are worth taking.
examples.professional: The banker reviewed our credit line and asked for updated revenue projections by Friday.
examples.analytical: A central banker must weigh the consequences of interest rate decisions for employment as well as for inflation.

nuance.analogy: A banker is like a gatekeeper of money, deciding which funds flow where and on what terms.
nuance.etymology: From bank plus the suffix -er.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the g in 'banker' as in 'bang-ger'.
Using 'banker' to mean a teller at the counter.
Confusing 'banker' with 'banquet', which is a formal dinner.

senses.definition: To be correct in one's judgment or statement about something. (This entry is a translation hub.)

core.definition: To be correct in your judgment, answer or statement about something.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on 'right'. The American r is a retroflex sound made by curling the tongue back, not a w, and 'right' is a diphthong that glides from ah to ee.

nuance.connotation: Neutral in most uses; it can sound smug or combative if you say 'I'm right' in an argument.
nuance.usage_note: In everyday talk Americans say 'You're right' to agree, or 'I think I'm right about that' when they are fairly sure. Saying 'I'm right' flatly in an argument can sound bossy or defensive. The phrase 'be right back' is a different idiom meaning you will return soon.

distinctions.note: More formal and neutral; it suits technical writing, exams and formal answers.
Used for measurements, data and information that match reality closely; it is common in data science.
Concerns reasons or actions being fair or defensible, not just factual correctness.

collocations: be right most of the time

examples.everyday: I think you were right about the traffic on Main Street, so let's take the back road.
examples.professional: I think you're right that the churn model is overfitting, so let's add regularization and recheck the validation scores.
examples.analytical: Aquinas was right to distinguish between knowing that God exists and knowing what God is in essence, since these are different kinds of knowledge.

nuance.analogy: Like a compass needle that points true north.
nuance.etymology: 'Right' comes from Old English 'riht', meaning straight or correct, from a Germanic root.
common_mistakes: Saying 'I am right' to sound confident in a debate, which can come across as aggressive; 'I think I'm right' is softer.
Confusing 'right' with 'write' or 'rite', which are homophones but have different meanings.
Using 'be right' for correctness of a calculation when 'be correct' or 'be accurate' is more precise in technical work.

senses.definition: That bears (some specified thing).
senses.example: a gift-bearing visitor

senses.definition: Of a beam, column, or other device, carrying weight or load.
senses.example: That's a bearing wall.

senses.definition: A mechanical device that supports another part or reduces friction.
senses.example: The wheel started squeaking because the bearing inside the axle had worn out.

senses.definition: One's understanding of one's orientation or relative position, literally or figuratively.
senses.example: Do we go left here or straight on? Hold on, let me just get my bearings.

senses.definition: Relevance; a relationship or connection.
senses.example: That has no bearing on this issue.

senses.definition: One's posture, demeanor, or manner.
senses.example: She walks with a confident, self-assured bearing.

senses.definition: The horizontal angle between the direction of an object and another object, or between it and that of true north; a heading or direction.
senses.example: The captain set a bearing of ninety degrees east and kept the ship on course.

senses.definition: That part of any member of a building which rests upon its supports.
senses.example: A lintel or beam may have four inches of bearing upon the wall.

senses.definition: The portion of a support on which anything rests.
senses.example: The engineer checked the bearing surface where the shaft rests against the housing.

senses.definition: The unsupported span.
senses.example: The beam has twenty feet of bearing between its supports.

senses.definition: Any single emblem or charge in an escutcheon or coat of arms.
senses.example: The heraldry expert identified each bearing on the shield, including the golden lion.

core.definition: One's sense of direction or position; how you orient yourself, literally or figuratively.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable. The final -ing is a short, quick i sound, not 'eeng', and the vowel in bear is the air sound.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. In phrases like 'get your bearings' it is positive or practical; in phrases about posture it can suggest dignity or composure.
nuance.usage_note: Americans most often use bearings in the phrases 'get your bearings' or 'lose your bearings,' meaning to figure out where you are or how a new situation works. 'Bearing' also describes how someone carries himself, as in 'calm bearing,' which is slightly formal. The mechanical sense of a ball bearing is common in engineering and car repair. A natural reply after a confusing day is 'I'm still getting my bearings.'

distinctions.note: Demeanor is how a person behaves or presents himself in a given moment; bearing is a more formal, settled posture and manner.
Baring is a homophone meaning uncovering or exposing; bearing as a noun means orientation or manner, so spelling matters.
Orientation is more formal and technical for awareness of place or self; bearings is the everyday phrase for it.

collocations: have a bearing on the decision

examples.everyday: It took me a few minutes to get my bearings after I got off the train in a new city.
examples.professional: Once the new team lead got her bearings, she set clear priorities for the sprint.
examples.analytical: A community that loses its theological bearings can drift toward whatever idea is most fashionable at the moment.

nuance.analogy: Like a ship's compass reading, your bearing tells you where you are in relation to everything around you.
nuance.etymology: From the verb bear; the navigational sense of direction comes from the idea of the course along which something is carried.
common_mistakes: Confusing bearing with baring, which is a homophone meaning to uncover or expose.
Saying 'I lost my bearing' for a single moment of confusion; Americans usually say 'lose my bearings' in the plural.

bearing.etymology: From Middle English *beringe*, *berynge*, *berende*, *berande*, *berand*, from Old English *berende* (“bearing; fruitful”), from Proto-Germanic **berandz*, present participle of Proto-Germanic **beraną* (“to bear; carry”), equivalent to *bear* + *ing*.

senses.definition: A very direct or quick path or trip.
senses.example: to make / strike a beeline for / to something

senses.definition: (historical) A dynamite fuse made with a small quantity of dynamite powder along its length, so that the spark travels quickly and at a specific known rate.
senses.example: The old quarry crew measured the beeline carefully so the blast would go off on schedule.
senses.label: historical

senses.definition: To travel in a straight line, ignoring established paths of travel.
senses.example: Once the bell rang, the kids beelined for the ice cream truck across the park.

core.definition: A very direct, fast path, usually said in the phrase 'make a beeline for' a place or person.

pronunciation.tip: Stress BEE, then say line with a long i. Keep the two parts clearly separated in sound, with the ee sound from bee and the i from line.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to lively. It describes eagerness or speed and can be friendly, though it may suggest someone is rushing rudely.
nuance.usage_note: Americans most often use beeline in the phrase 'make a beeline for' something, such as the snack table or the exit. It is informal and suggests moving directly and quickly. As a verb, 'beeline' means to go straight somewhere, and it is common in casual conversation, not in formal writing.

distinctions.note: A straight line is a neutral geometric or physical description, while a beeline also suggests urgency or purpose.
A shortcut saves time by taking a different route, while a beeline is a direct route with no detours.

examples.everyday: As soon as the pizza came out, the kids made a beeline for the kitchen.
examples.professional: After the meeting ended, the vice president made a beeline for the coffee machine, so we had to catch her in the hallway.
examples.analytical: To make a beeline is to choose the shortest path toward a goal, which suggests a single-minded will that ignores the usual detours of social life.

nuance.analogy: A beeline is like an arrow shot straight at the target, skipping all the side paths.
nuance.etymology: From the old observation that bees fly straight from the hive to flowers, in the sense of a direct line.
common_mistakes: Writing 'bee line' as two words in casual speech, although one word is common.
Using beeline without a preposition, as in 'beeline the door', when 'make a beeline for the door' is more natural.

beeline.etymology: From *bee* + *line*, due to the belief that a bee returns to its hive in a straight course, originally an Americanism.

senses.definition: In a belated manner; tardily.
senses.example: The city belatedly repaired the potholes after residents complained for months.

core.definition: Later than expected or appropriate; after the proper time has already passed.

pronunciation.tip: Stress LAY. The middle syllable is a quick, reduced id sound, and the final syllable is lee, not 'lay'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It reports a late action, often with a hint of 'finally' or of regret that it came so late.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use it in news reports and polite speech, as in 'He belatedly admitted the mistake.' In casual conversation, 'finally' or 'late' is more common. It fits best in formal writing, where a late action needs describing without blame.

distinctions.note: Finally signals the end of a long wait; belatedly stresses that the action came too late to be ideal.
Eventually means in the end after a process; belatedly implies a failure of timing.

examples.everyday: My brother belatedly remembered my birthday, so he called at eleven at night.
examples.professional: The vendor belatedly sent the security patch, so we had to delay the release by a week.
examples.analytical: The committee belatedly acknowledged the flaw in its methodology, after the published results had already shaped policy.

nuance.analogy: Like a train that reaches the station after everyone has gone home.
nuance.etymology: From belated plus the adverb ending -ly; belated comes from be- and late.
common_mistakes: Stressing the wrong syllable: it is bih-LAY-tid-lee, not bih-lay-TID-lee.
Using it for everyday lateness, such as 'I belatedly arrived at work'; for that, 'late' is natural.

senses.definition: That belittles; condescending.
Belittlement.
senses.example: Her belittling of my ideas in front of clients was unprofessional and unkind.

core.definition: Making someone feel unimportant or less capable, often in a condescending way.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on LIT, and the middle syllable is reduced to uh. Do not stress the -ling ending, which is a short ih sound.

nuance.connotation: Negative. A belittling remark or tone hurts the listener's sense of worth.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use belittling for remarks, tone, or behavior: 'That comment was belittling.' It is common in workplace, school, and relationship talk. It is stronger than rude and less formal than condescending. As a noun, belittling is rare; people say belittlement.

distinctions.note: Condescending describes a polite-seeming attitude of superiority, while belittling describes remarks or actions that actually make someone feel smaller.
Demeaning means lowering someone's dignity or status, and it often refers to a situation or task, while belittling refers to what someone says or does.
Dismissive means refusing to take someone seriously, while belittling goes further by actively making them seem small.

examples.everyday: Don't take it personally, but that joke was kind of belittling.
examples.professional: Please avoid belittling language in code reviews and focus on the code itself.
examples.analytical: The belittling tone of the report undermined an otherwise careful argument.

nuance.analogy: Like a tape measure that always reads short: each comment makes the person look smaller than they really are.
nuance.etymology: From belittle, from be- plus little, with the suffix -ing.
common_mistakes: Saying I feel belittling; use I feel belittled for how you feel and belittling for the remark or behavior.
Using belittling as a noun in everyday speech, where belittlement or put-downs is more natural.

senses.definition: The characteristic of being bellicose.
senses.example: The senator's bellicosity during the hearing alarmed both parties' staff members.

core.definition: An aggressive, hostile, or warlike attitude or behavior; a tendency to fight or provoke conflict.

pronunciation.tip: The stress moves to the third syllable, KAH, in the -cos- part, so it does not stay on the first syllable like bellicose. Americans pronounce the first o in cot like ah, and the final -ity is a short ih-tee.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It names a hostile or warlike disposition, often in nations, leaders, or groups.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use bellicosity in news analysis, political writing, and academic discussions about conflict. In casual conversation, people usually say hostility, aggression, or a fighting attitude. It sounds stiff in everyday talk, so reserve it for formal descriptions.

distinctions.note: Aggression is the general word for forceful or hostile behavior. Bellicosity suggests a more deliberate, war-like tendency or temperament.
Hostility is a feeling of antagonism, while bellicosity is an active readiness to fight or provoke.

examples.everyday: I could feel the bellicosity in the room as soon as the two neighbors started arguing about the fence.
examples.professional: The team's bellicosity during code reviews drove away two good engineers last quarter.
examples.analytical: Hobbes locates human bellicosity not in innate evil but in competition, diffidence, and the desire for glory.

nuance.analogy: Bellicosity is like static electricity in a room: you do not see it, but you feel it the moment someone reaches out.
nuance.etymology: From bellicose plus the noun suffix -ity, from Latin bellicosus, warlike.
common_mistakes: Writing the stress on the wrong syllable, as in BEL-ih-kos-i-tee.
Confusing it with bellicose in a sentence where the noun is required, such as His bellicose was obvious.

senses.definition: To bend one's upper body forward and down while standing or kneeling.
senses.example: I had to bend over to see all the way down there.

senses.definition: To act submissively.
senses.example: You really bend over when the boss comes calling, don't you?

senses.definition: Used other than figuratively or idiomatically: see bent,‎ over.
senses.example: Sandrita was bent over the sink doing the dishes.

core.definition: To bend your upper body forward and down, for example to pick something up or to look at something closely.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on OH in over, while bent is lighter. The final -er is an unstressed r-colored vowel, not 'oh-vair'. In fast speech the t of bent may flap, so it can sound like 'ben-DOH-ver'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral for the physical action; the figurative sense of submitting or acting servile is negative.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use bent over literally to describe posture: bent over the sink, bent over to tie a shoe. The figurative sense of submission is rare in everyday speech. The idiom bend over backwards, meaning to try very hard to help, is much more common.

distinctions.note: Bend over is the base or present form, as in 'I bend over to pick it up'; bent over is the past form, as in 'I was bent over the sink'.
Lean over means tilting the upper body toward something, often with support; bent over suggests a fuller, more folded posture.

collocations: bent over to tie her shoes

examples.everyday: I was bent over the kitchen sink when the phone rang.
examples.professional: He was bent over the server rack swapping a failed drive while we waited on the call.
examples.analytical: The painting shows the farmer bent over the field, an image that makes the burden of labor visible in the body.

nuance.analogy: Like a folding chair, the body bends at the hip and folds forward.
nuance.etymology: From Old English bendan, 'to bend', and ofer, 'over, above'.
common_mistakes: Using bent over for the present tense; say 'I bend over' and use 'bent over' only for the past.
Confusing it with lean over, which describes a lighter tilt, often with support.

senses.definition: A well-defined procedure that is known to produce near-optimum results.
senses.example: Our team adopted a best practice of code review before every merge to production.

core.definition: A proven method or procedure that reliably produces the best results, often recommended as the standard way to do something in a field or workplace.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on the second word, PRAK, with a lighter stress on best. The final syllable of practice is short, like 'tiss', not 'tees' or 'tice'.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It sounds authoritative and professional, though it can sound like jargon in casual talk.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use best practice in meetings, reports, and emails to mean a recommended way of doing something that has been shown to work. In casual conversation it can sound like corporate jargon, so 'what works best' or 'the standard approach' is more natural. People often say 'follow best practices,' 'adopt a best practice,' or 'share best practices.'

distinctions.note: Standard is a typical or required level of performance; best practice is a recommended method that has been shown to work well.
A guideline is flexible advice; best practice implies the method is already proven and widely accepted in the field.

examples.everyday: The best practice with a cast-iron pan is to dry it right away so it doesn't rust.
examples.professional: Let's follow best practice and add a code review before anything gets merged into main.
examples.analytical: Whether a rule counts as best practice should depend on evidence, not tradition alone, so each claim needs justification.

nuance.analogy: Like a recipe that many experienced cooks have tested and trust.
nuance.etymology: Best from Old English betst; practice from Old French pratique, from Latin practica.
common_mistakes: Using the singular 'best practice' when you mean several methods; in lists Americans usually say 'best practices.'
Stressing best as strongly as practice; the main stress is on the second word.

conversation.text: It's best practice to back up your files every day.
Can you share some best practices for running remote meetings?
We follow industry best practices for data security.

core.definition: In the Bible, a Persian-era name for a family head who returned from Babylonian exile with Zerubbabel and Ezra; his descendants are listed among the returnees.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, and the final syllable rhymes with 'eye'. The 'g' is a hard 'g' as in 'big', and the 'v' is a normal English 'v'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral, used only as a biblical name.
nuance.usage_note: Bigvai is a name you meet in Ezra and Nehemiah, usually in lists of returning exiles. Americans encounter it in Bible study or reference works and rarely use it otherwise.

examples.everyday: I was reading Ezra last night and got stuck on the long lists of names, like Bigvai, who came back from exile.
examples.professional: In the sermon, the pastor noted that Bigvai appears in the lists of those who returned with Zerubbabel, which shows the community was rebuilt by families.
examples.analytical: The genealogical lists in Ezra 2 and Nehemiah 7, which include the sons of Bigvai, function as a register of the restored community and its claim to continuity.

nuance.analogy: Bigvai is like a name on an old census roll, recorded so that a returning family could be counted as part of the community.
nuance.etymology: Persian personal name, meaning uncertain according to most sources.
common_mistakes: Stressing the second syllable, as in 'big-VYE'.
Pronouncing the 'g' as a soft 'j' sound.
nuance.biblical_note: Ezra 2:2 and Nehemiah 7:7 list Bigvai among leaders who returned from Babylon with Zerubbabel. Ezra 2:14 records the sons of Bigvai as part of the returning families. Ezra 8:14 names later members of the family who joined Ezra's return to Jerusalem.

senses.definition: To end a column of stitches by trapping its final stitch in a way that prevents unraveling.
senses.example: When the scarf reached full length, I bound off the last row of stitches.

senses.definition: A technique used to bind off stitches.
senses.example: I’ve learned a new bind off that’s perfect for cuffs and brims of hats.

core.definition: To finish a row of knitting or crocheting by working the last stitches so they form a secure edge that cannot unravel.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on OFF, the particle, not on bind. The final d in bind is often barely released before the vowel of off, so it sounds close to 'bine-DAWF'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it is a plain, practical instruction.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say 'bind off' for finishing a knitted edge, and knitters in the US use the term in patterns and classes. British knitters usually say 'cast off' for the same technique. Natural replies include 'Okay, I'll bind off at the end of the row' or 'Did you bind off yet?'

distinctions.note: Same technique; 'cast off' is common in British knitting, while Americans normally say 'bind off'.
Cast on starts a set of stitches at the beginning of a project, while bind off finishes them at the end.

examples.everyday: I'm almost done with the scarf, I just need to bind off the last row.
examples.professional: The pattern says to bind off after the decrease rows, so please check the sample before we send it to production.
examples.analytical: A knitted edge is only as stable as its bind-off, because a row that is too tight or too loose determines whether the garment keeps its shape.

nuance.analogy: Binding off is like tying the end of a shoelace so the loops cannot slip out.
nuance.etymology: 'Bind' comes from Old English bindan, and 'off' comes from Old English of.
common_mistakes: Saying 'bind up' or 'bind out' instead of 'bind off'.
Writing 'bind of' instead of 'bind off'.
Stressing BIND in the phrase instead of OFF.

senses.definition: A coefficient of any of the terms in the expansion of the binomial (x+y), defined by (nk)=n!k!(n−k)!, read as "n choose k"

core.definition: The number of ways to choose k items from n without regard to order, the coefficient of a term in the expansion of (x + y) to the nth power; read 'n choose k'.

pronunciation.tip: The phrase has its strongest stress on FISH in coefficient, while binomial keeps a secondary stress on NOH. Say the middle of coefficient as a quick uh, not as separate ef syllables.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a precise mathematical term.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use binomial coefficient almost only in math, statistics, and computer science, and they often write it as C(n,k) or nCk. In US classrooms, people say 'n choose k' aloud as the standard reading. Outside technical settings the phrase would sound very specialized.

distinctions.note: A binomial coefficient is the number produced by the formula, while combination is the concept of choosing a group without order that the coefficient counts.
A permutation counts arrangements where order matters, so for the same n and k it is larger than the binomial coefficient.

examples.everyday: My son asked me what a binomial coefficient was for his homework, so I had to look it up on my phone.
examples.professional: The feature code calls a library function for binomial coefficients, so we do not have to write the factorial math ourselves.
examples.analytical: The binomial coefficient counts the subsets of size k drawn from n elements, which is why it appears in the expansion of (x + y) to the nth power.

nuance.analogy: It is a counting shortcut: how many different teams of three you can pick from ten players, when the order of picking does not matter.
nuance.etymology: Combines binomial (bi- 'two' plus Latin nomen 'name') with coefficient (Latin co- 'together' plus efficere 'to produce').
common_mistakes: Writing n!/k! instead of n!/(k!(n-k)!), which drops the denominator factor.
Putting the strongest stress on BYE at the start instead of FISH in coefficient.

senses.definition: Of or pertaining to biogenesis.
Of or pertaining to biogenetics.

core.definition: Relating to biogenesis, or to the biological processes by which living matter or organic compounds are produced.

pronunciation.tip: The primary stress is on NET, the third syllable, not on the oh. The reduced uh sound in the middle is quick, and the final -ic is pronounced as ik.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and scientific. It describes processes rather than judging them.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use biogenetic almost only in chemistry, biology, and origin-of-life research, often in academic writing. It is not the same as genetic, which means related to heredity. Most people would use a plainer phrase like 'the way living things make molecules' in conversation.

distinctions.note: Genetic refers to heredity and genes. Biogenetic refers to how living matter or organic molecules are produced by biological processes.
Biogenic describes something that is produced by living organisms. Biogenetic is more about the process or theory of how it arises.

examples.everyday: My sister is studying biogenetic processes in graduate school, and I still can't explain them at dinner.
examples.professional: The lab's biogenetic pathway model predicts which enzymes produce the compound, so we can prioritize them for testing.
examples.analytical: Any biogenetic account of the origin of life must explain how simple molecules became self-replicating systems.

nuance.analogy: A biogenetic pathway is like an assembly line: each station adds one part until the finished product comes off the end.
nuance.etymology: From bio- (Greek bios, life) and genetic (Greek genetikos, relating to origin).
common_mistakes: Confusing biogenetic with genetic, which refers to heredity rather than the production of living matter.
Stressing the first syllable (BYE-oh-juh-net-ik) instead of the -NET syllable.

senses.definition: A violent gust of wind (in windy weather) or apparent wind (around a moving vehicle).
senses.example: A cold blast of wind rattled the windows of the old farmhouse.

senses.definition: A forcible stream of gas or liquid from an orifice, for example from a bellows, the tuyeres of a blast furnace, a person's mouth, etc.
senses.example: A blast of air from the bellows made the campfire roar back to life.

senses.definition: A hit of a recreational drug from a pipe.
senses.example: He took one blast from the pipe and then sat silently on the couch.

senses.definition: The continuous blowing to which one charge of ore or metal is subjected in a furnace.
senses.example: Many tons of iron were melted at a blast.

senses.definition: The exhaust steam from an engine, driving a column of air out of a boiler chimney, and thus creating an intense draught through the fire; also, any draught produced by the blast.
senses.example: The old steam engine's blast pulled hot air through the boiler fire.

senses.definition: An explosion, especially for the purpose of destroying a mass of rock, etc.
senses.example: arc blast

senses.definition: A verbal attack or punishment; a severe criticism or reprimand.
senses.example: My manager gave me a blast yesterday for coming in late.

senses.definition: An explosive charge for blasting.
senses.example: The crew set a blast in the quarry wall to clear the rock.

senses.definition: A loud, sudden sound.
Unwanted noise from a microphone.
senses.example: A loud blast of static from the microphone interrupted the keynote speech.

senses.definition: A sudden pernicious effect, as if by a noxious wind, especially on animals and plants; a blight.
senses.example: A sudden blast swept through the orchard and withered the apple blossoms overnight.

senses.definition: A good time; an enjoyable moment.
senses.example: We had a blast at the party last night.

senses.definition: A promotional message sent to an entire mailing list.
senses.example: an e-mail blast; a fax blast

senses.definition: A flatulent disease of sheep.
senses.example: The farmer worried that the lambs had caught the blast from the wet pasture.

senses.definition: A period of full dosage of PEDs as opposed to a period of reduced intake.
senses.example: blast and cruise

senses.definition: An immature or undifferentiated cell (e.g. lymphoblast, myeloblast).
senses.example: The pathologist identified leukemia by counting blasts in the bone marrow sample.

senses.definition: A direct and fast swing of a bat; a home run.
senses.example: His late-inning blast over the left-field wall won the game for the Yankees.

senses.definition: To make an impression on, by making a loud blast or din.
senses.example: The brass band blasted the crowd with a fanfare that made everyone jump.

senses.definition: To make a loud noise.
senses.example: The ferry horn blasted across the harbor at dawn, waking the entire neighborhood.

senses.definition: To play (music) very loudly out of a speaker.
senses.example: My roommate blasts hip-hop from his speaker every night while I'm studying.

senses.definition: To shatter, as if by an explosion.
senses.example: The explosion blasted the lab's windows into shards across the parking lot.

senses.definition: To open up a hole in, usually by means of a sudden and imprecise method (such as an explosion).
senses.example: Blast right through it.

senses.definition: To curse; to damn.
senses.example: Blast it! Foiled again.

senses.definition: To shoot, especially with an energy weapon (as opposed to one which fires projectiles).
senses.example: Chewbacca blasted the Stormtroopers with his laser rifle.

senses.definition: To shoot; kick the ball in hope of scoring a goal.
senses.example: He blasted the ball past the goalkeeper in the final minute of the match.

senses.definition: To shoot; to attack or shoot (someone or a place).
senses.example: They showed up blasting.

senses.definition: To criticize or reprimand severely; to verbally discipline or punish.
senses.example: My manager suddenly blasted me yesterday for being a little late to work for five days in a row, because I was never getting myself up on time.

senses.definition: To bring destruction or ruin on; to destroy.
senses.example: The hurricane blasted the coastal town, leaving nothing standing but the church steeple.

senses.definition: To blight or wither.
senses.example: A cold wind blasted the rose plants.

senses.definition: To have a period of full dosage of PEDs as opposed to reducing them during a cruise period.
senses.example: blast and cruise

senses.definition: To cover in tattoos.
senses.example: I don't have the balls to get my face blasted like a rapper.

senses.definition: To run a nucleotide sequence (for nucleic acids) or an amino acid sequence (for proteins) through a BLAST (Basic Local Alignment Search Tool).
Used to show anger or disappointment: damn.

core.definition: A sudden, powerful explosion, a strong rush of air, or a very loud sound, or a very enjoyable time in informal speech.

pronunciation.tip: It is one syllable with a short a and a final st cluster. Do not insert a vowel before the s or the t, as in 'blas-it'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral in most senses, but it can be positive in 'have a blast' and negative when describing destruction or a cold wind.
nuance.usage_note: Americans often say 'I had a blast' or 'we had a blast' to mean they had great fun. They also say 'full blast' for the highest volume, as in 'the heater is on full blast'. 'A blast from the past' is a common phrase for an unexpected reminder of someone or something from earlier times.

distinctions.note: An explosion is the event itself, while blast can refer to the force of the explosion or to a short, powerful burst of air or sound.
A gust is a brief, sudden rush of wind that is usually weaker than a blast, while a blast can be stronger and more intense.
Boom refers to a deep, resonant sound, while blast suggests a sharp, powerful burst of force or noise.

examples.everyday: We had a blast at the lake this weekend, even though the wind was a little cold.
examples.professional: The sales conference was a blast, and the team said they want to repeat it next year.
examples.analytical: Every blast of rhetoric in that debate reveals an argument that is more about feeling than evidence.

nuance.analogy: Like opening a door onto a winter storm, when cold air rushes in all at once.
nuance.etymology: From Old English blæst, meaning a blowing or a gust of wind, related to the Germanic root of blow.
common_mistakes: Using blast with the wrong preposition, as in 'blast at full volume' instead of 'full blast'.
Mixing up 'have a blast' with 'make a blast', which is not a natural phrase.
Confusing blast with bust or blasted when speaking about a loud noise.

blast.etymology: Middle English *blast*, from Old English *blǣst* (“blowing, blast”), from **blāstu*, from Proto-Germanic **blēstuz* (“blowing, blast”).

senses.definition: In a blatant manner; so as to be highly visible or obvious.
senses.example: Although he was blatantly on drugs, the crowd still cheered him.

core.definition: In an obvious and unashamed way, so that everyone can see that something wrong is happening.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, BLAY. The -tant- part is quick and weak, and the final -ly is a light lee.

nuance.connotation: Negative; it implies that someone is doing something wrong openly and without shame.
nuance.usage_note: Americans often use blatantly with verbs such as lie, ignore, copy or favor. In casual speech people also say blatantly obvious, which is lighter and only means very clear. The word is common in news and conversation about unfair or dishonest behavior.

distinctions.note: Openly means without hiding; blatantly adds that the action is shameless or wrong.
Clearly is neutral; blatantly signals that something bad is being done in plain view.
Obviously is about how easy something is to see; blatantly is about shamelessness or offensiveness.

examples.everyday: The guy at the next table was blatantly staring at my food.
examples.professional: Two vendors blatantly ignored the security requirements, so we're flagging them in the audit.
examples.analytical: The author blatantly misreads Aquinas, reducing his distinctions between kinds of being to a single crude claim.

nuance.analogy: Like a shoplifter walking out with the item in plain sight: the boldness is part of the offense.
nuance.etymology: From the adjective blatant plus the adverbial ending -ly.
common_mistakes: Using blatantly obvious in formal writing where clearly or plainly would be more precise.
Confusing blatantly with blandly, which means dull or mild.

senses.definition: Unable to see, or only partially able to see.
senses.example: Even a blind hen sometimes finds a grain of corn.

senses.definition: Failing to recognize, acknowledge or perceive.
senses.example: The lovers were blind to each other’s faults.

senses.definition: Having little or no visibility.
senses.example: a blind path

senses.definition: Closed at one end; having a dead end; exitless.
senses.example: a blind alley

senses.definition: Having no openings for light or passage; both dark and exitless.
senses.example: a blind wall

senses.definition: Able to be fixed without access to one end.
senses.example: a blind rivet

senses.definition: Smallest or slightest.
senses.example: I shouted, but he didn’t take a blind bit of notice.

senses.definition: Without any prior knowledge.
senses.example: He took a blind guess at which fork in the road would take him to the airport.

senses.definition: Unconditional; without regard to evidence, logic, reality, accidental mistakes, extenuating circumstances, etc.
senses.example: blind deference

senses.definition: Using blinded study design, wherein information is purposely limited to prevent bias.
senses.example: a blind trial

senses.definition: Unintelligible or illegible.
senses.example: a blind passage in a book; blind writing

senses.definition: (Of a pimple) not having a well-defined head.
senses.example: The dermatologist said the pimple was blind, so no drainage was needed.

senses.definition: Abortive; failing to produce flowers or fruit.
senses.example: blind buds

senses.definition: Uncircumcised.
senses.example: The medieval text used blind to describe an uncircumcised man, a term now obsolete.

senses.definition: A movable covering for a window to keep out light, made of cloth or of narrow slats that can block light or allow it to pass.
senses.example: We pulled down the blind to keep the afternoon sun out of the living room.

senses.definition: A destination sign mounted on a public transport vehicle displaying the route destination, number, name and/or via points, etc.
senses.example: The bus blind read 'Downtown Express' and I hopped on before the doors closed.

senses.definition: A place where people can hide in order to observe wildlife.
senses.example: a duck blind

senses.definition: Something to mislead the eye or the understanding, or to conceal some covert deed or design; a subterfuge, deception.
senses.example: His friendly chatter was a blind to hide the fact that he had already sold the house.

senses.definition: A hiding place.
senses.example: The kids used the abandoned shed as a blind during hide-and-seek.

senses.definition: The blindside.
senses.example: The defender came from the blind and tackled the striker before he saw him.

senses.definition: A forced bet: the small blind or the big blind.
senses.example: The blinds are $10 and $20, and the ante is $1.

senses.definition: A player who is forced to pay such a bet.
senses.example: The blinds immediately folded when I reraised.

senses.definition: A blindage.
senses.example: The engineers built a blind of steel plate to shield the crew from debris.

senses.definition: No score.
senses.example: At halftime, the scoreboard still showed a blind for both teams.

senses.definition: To make temporarily or permanently blind.
senses.example: The light was so bright that for a moment he was blinded.

senses.definition: To darken; to obscure to the eye or understanding; to conceal.
senses.example: Thick smoke blinded the valley, obscuring the road and the last glimmer of sun.

senses.definition: To cover with a thin coating of sand and fine gravel, for example a road newly paved, in order that the joints between the stones may be filled.
senses.example: The crew blinded the newly paved road with sand so the stones would lock together.

senses.definition: Without seeing; unseeingly.
senses.example: He had to drive blind through the fog, trusting only the dashed center line.

senses.definition: Absolutely, totally.
senses.example: to swear blind

senses.definition: Without looking at the cards dealt.
senses.example: In the poker game, Tom bet blind, without looking at the cards he had been dealt.

senses.definition: As a pastry case only, without any filling.
senses.example: Blind bake your pie case for fifteen minutes, then add the filling. This will help avoid a “soggy bottom”.

core.definition: Unable to see, or only able to see very poorly. Also describes not noticing or refusing to notice something obvious.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the single syllable and use the long i diphthong, as in mind. The final d is clear, so do not say bland, which has a different vowel.

nuance.connotation: Neutral in the literal sense. It can be negative when used figuratively, as in blind to a problem, and it is sensitive when used for people.
nuance.usage_note: In formal writing and official contexts Americans prefer person who is blind or visually impaired rather than the blind man or the blind. In casual speech blind is common and fine. The figurative use, blind to a problem, is everyday American English. Phrases like blind date and blind review are standard.

distinctions.note: Visually impaired is a formal, official term that covers partial sight. Blind is more direct and common in everyday talk, and in the US it can mean legally blind with very limited sight.
Sightless is more literary and poetic. Blind is the normal everyday word.
Ignorant means lacking knowledge. Blind means unable or unwilling to perceive something that is visible or obvious.

examples.everyday: My grandfather is nearly blind, but he still reads the paper with a magnifying glass.
examples.professional: We ran a blind review, so the scorers never saw which team submitted each model.
examples.analytical: Paul says the unbeliever is blinded by the god of this world, unable to perceive spiritual truth without the Spirit.

nuance.analogy: Being blind to a problem is like wearing a pair of sunglasses at night: the problem is there, but you cannot see it.
nuance.etymology: From Old English blind, from Proto-Germanic *blindaz, meaning unable to see.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing blind with the vowel of bland, saying BLAND.
Using the blind as the standard noun in formal writing, where person who is blind sounds more respectful.
nuance.biblical_note: The Hebrew word 'iwwer and the Greek word tuphlos both mean blind, and both are used literally and figuratively in Scripture. Isaiah 35:5 (RSV) promises that the eyes of the blind shall be opened as part of God's restoration. John 9:1-41 (RSV) tells the story of a man born blind whom Jesus heals, and the chapter turns on whether spiritual sight or physical sight matters most. Matthew 15:14 (RSV) calls the Pharisees blind guides who lead the blind into a pit.

blind.etymology: From Middle English *blynd*, from Old English *blind*, from **blind*, from Proto-Germanic **blindaz*.

senses.definition: A person who blows.
senses.example: My grandfather was a steady blower on the glassworks floor, shaping hot bottles all day.

senses.definition: A fissure from which firedamp issues, often in quantity for many years.
senses.example: Miners feared the blower that vented methane from the seam, hissing day after day.

senses.definition: Any device that blows; often, especially, a furnace component or a supercharger.
senses.example: The race car's supercharger blower whined loudly as the driver accelerated out of the turn.

senses.definition: A ducted fan, usually part of a heating, ventilation, and/or air conditioning system.
senses.example: The technician replaced the worn blower in the air handler, which had been rattling for weeks.

senses.definition: A small fish of the Atlantic coast, Sphoeroides maculatus; the puffer.
senses.example: Anglers on the pier caught a small blower that puffed up when lifted from the water.

senses.definition: A gun.
senses.example: The gangster pulled a blower from his coat and told everyone in the bar to freeze.

senses.definition: The whale; so called from its habit of spouting up a column of water.
senses.example: On the whale-watching tour, the guide pointed to a blower spouting a tall column of spray.

senses.definition: (dated) A braggart, or loud talker.
senses.example: Uncle Walt was a blower who never stopped bragging about the fish he almost caught.
senses.label: dated

core.definition: A machine or device that forces air out in a strong stream, such as a leaf blower, snow blower or the fan in a furnace.

pronunciation.tip: Two syllables, with stress on the first. The final -er is a weak, r-colored vowel, so it sounds like 'BLOH-er', not 'BLOH-wer'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It describes equipment and carries no emotional meaning.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'blower' mainly in compounds such as leaf blower and snow blower, and in home heating talk about the furnace blower. For hair they say 'blow dryer' or 'hair dryer,' not 'hair blower.' A person who blows is rarely called a blower in everyday speech.

distinctions.note: A fan moves air by spinning blades to cool a room, while a blower forces air through a duct or nozzle, often with more pressure.
A blow dryer is a handheld appliance for hair, while blower is a general word for a machine that pushes air.
A vacuum pulls air and debris in, while a blower pushes air out.

examples.everyday: I'll grab the leaf blower and clear the patio before the guests arrive.
examples.professional: The furnace blower failed overnight, so the warehouse lost heat before the morning shift.
examples.analytical: In a supercharged engine, the blower compresses the intake air so that more fuel and oxygen can burn in each cycle.

nuance.analogy: A blower is like a fan with muscle: it pushes air harder through a narrow passage.
nuance.etymology: From blow, Old English blāwan, plus the suffix -er meaning a thing or person that does something.
common_mistakes: Saying 'hair blower' instead of 'blow dryer' or 'hair dryer'.
Pronouncing the final syllable as a full 'wer' sound instead of a weak r-colored vowel.

blower.etymology: From Middle English *blowere*, *blower*, from Old English *blāwere*; equivalent to *blow* + *er*.

senses.definition: One who boasts; a braggart.
senses.example: Nobody liked the office boaster, who always claimed credit for other people's work.

senses.definition: A stonemason's broad-faced chisel.
senses.example: The stonemason reached for a boaster to smooth the broad face of the slab.

core.definition: A person who talks proudly and too much about his or her own achievements, possessions or abilities.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable. The st cluster is one clean sound with no extra vowel, and the final -er is a reduced r-colored schwa.

nuance.connotation: Negative. Calling someone a boaster is an insult that suggests they are annoying or vain.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use boaster and braggart for someone who brags, usually in a teasing or disapproving way. Boaster is the everyday word; braggart sounds stronger or more literary. Among friends it can be playful, but in professional settings it is a judgment, so avoid it there. The sense of a stonemason's chisel belongs to craft contexts and is rarely used otherwise.

distinctions.note: Braggart is stronger and more literary; boaster is the everyday word for someone who brags.
A show-off seeks attention through display, while a boaster specifically talks about his or her own successes.

examples.everyday: Dan is a boaster, so don't be surprised when he tells you his fishing story for the fifth time.
examples.professional: Our team lead is no boaster; she gives credit to the people who did the work.
examples.analytical: The boaster often mistakes noise for strength, and his speech reveals the insecurity it is meant to hide.

nuance.analogy: Like a rooster that crows loudest from the fence, announcing itself rather than the work.
nuance.etymology: From boast (verb), of uncertain origin, plus the agent suffix -er.
