'Leak' is informal and often implies that information escaped without permission, whereas 'divulgence' is more formal and can be deliberate.

examples.professional: The security review flagged the divulgence of customer records to an unapproved vendor.
examples.analytical: The ethical question turns on whether the divulgence of confidential information can ever be justified.

nuance.analogy: A divulgence is like opening a sealed envelope that was meant for one reader only: the contents are now out in the open.
nuance.etymology: From Latin divulgare, to make public, from di- (apart) and vulgare (to make common).
common_mistakes: Use 'divulge' as a verb ('divulge a secret'), not 'divulgence' as a verb.
Do not confuse 'divulge' with 'divide'; they are unrelated words.

core.definition: In the Bible, an Edomite servant of King Saul who reported David's visit to the priests at Nob and later killed them.

pronunciation.tip: The stress is on the first syllable, DOH, and the second syllable is a short 'ig' as in 'pig'. Don't stress the second syllable.

nuance.connotation: Negative; he is remembered as a betrayer who carried out violence against innocent priests.
nuance.usage_note: Americans mention Doeg mainly in Bible study, sermons, or seminary discussion. He is not a common everyday name. When naming him in conversation, say 'Doeg the Edomite' to make clear who you mean.

distinctions.note: Abiathar was a priest who escaped the massacre at Nob and joined David, while Doeg was the one who carried out the killing.

examples.everyday: Our Bible study was on 1 Samuel, and we spent a while on Doeg, the man who turned on the priests.
examples.professional: In the sermon, Doeg served as the example of a courtier who betrays the innocent to win favor.
examples.analytical: The narrative presents Doeg as the instrument of Saul's cruelty, and Psalm 52 uses his story to warn against trusting in riches and in evil speech.

nuance.analogy: Doeg is like an informer who names the innocent to a powerful boss, then carries out the punishment himself.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the name as 'Dog' with a short vowel; the vowel is a long 'oh'.
Confusing Doeg with Abiathar, who was the priest who survived the attack at Nob.
nuance.biblical_note: Doeg is an Edomite who served as chief herdsman for King Saul. In 1 Samuel 21:7 he is at the sanctuary at Nob when David arrives, and he later reports David's visit to Saul in 1 Samuel 22:9–10. In 1 Samuel 22:18–19 he kills eighty-five priests at Nob on Saul's command, and Psalm 52 is titled as a psalm written about his betrayal.

senses.definition: To treat something as dogma.
senses.example: Some professors dogmatize their favorite theories and refuse to consider any new evidence.

senses.definition: To speak or write dogmatically.
senses.example: In the debate he kept dogmatizing, repeating his claims without offering a single supporting argument.

core.definition: To state opinions or beliefs as absolutely true, without proof, openness, or willingness to discuss them.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable: DAWG-muh-tyz. The second syllable is reduced to a schwa, and the -ize ending is pronounced like 'tyze', with no separate syllable for the i.

nuance.connotation: Negative; it implies arrogance or a refusal to consider other views.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use dogmatize mainly in academic, philosophical, religious, or serious opinion writing. In casual speech people say someone is 'preaching' or 'laying down the law.' The word works well in a critical review or essay, but in conversation it would sound stiff.

distinctions.note: Assert is neutral and means to state firmly; dogmatize adds the criticism that the statement is treated as beyond question.
Pontificate means to speak in a pompous, self-important way; dogmatize focuses on presenting claims as unquestionable.

examples.everyday: I wish he wouldn't dogmatize about every restaurant; sometimes he just has a bad night.
examples.professional: Our architect dogmatized about the cloud stack, so the team stopped asking whether a simpler design might work.
examples.analytical: Scholars should not dogmatize about contested texts when the manuscript evidence remains incomplete and ambiguous.

nuance.analogy: To dogmatize is to nail a hypothesis to the wall and refuse to let anyone take it down for inspection.
nuance.etymology: From Greek dogmatizein, to hold or teach as doctrine, from dogma.
common_mistakes: Treating dogmatize as a neutral verb for speaking; it usually carries criticism.
Pronouncing the stress on the second syllable, as in dog-MA-tize.

senses.definition: Ellipsis of don't count your chickens before they're hatched.

core.definition: Do not assume good results will happen before they actually do, because plans can still fail.

pronunciation.tip: 'Your' is usually reduced to 'yer' in fast speech, and 'chickens' is stressed on its first syllable. Link the words so 'don't count' sounds like 'dohn-KOWNT'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to cautionary; it can sound wise or mildly preachy depending on tone.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say this when someone is celebrating too early, such as before a job offer is signed or a deal closes. Said kindly, it is friendly advice, but said bluntly it can sound like criticism of someone's optimism. A natural reply is 'Yeah, I know, I'm just excited' or 'Fair point, I'll wait until it's official'.

distinctions.note: Don't jinx it is superstitious, implying that talking about good luck will cause bad luck, while this proverb warns against assuming outcomes without evidence.

distinctions.vs: don't put all your eggs in one basket
distinctions.note: That proverb is about spreading risk, while this proverb is about premature optimism.

collocations: too early to count your chickens
count your chickens before they hatch
a little premature to count your chickens

examples.everyday: You got into the grad program? Congrats! Just don't count your chickens yet until you see the funding letter.
examples.professional: The client said they'll probably sign, but let's not count our chickens until the contract is countersigned.
examples.analytical: Economists caution against counting chickens before they hatch when they project growth from a single quarter of strong earnings.

nuance.analogy: Like planning a big feast from eggs still in the nest.
nuance.etymology: Old proverb of uncertain origin; the earliest form is unclear.
common_mistakes: Dropping 'your' or 'before they hatch' in casual speech, which can make the meaning unclear.
Taking it literally about farming or counting animals rather than premature hope.
Stressing the word 'chickens' incorrectly, as if it were chick-EENS.

senses.definition: The characteristic of being dowdy; frumpiness; plainness.
senses.example: Critics mocked the dowdiness of the museum's uniforms, calling them drab and shapeless.

core.definition: The quality of looking dull, old-fashioned, or unattractive, especially in clothing or style; frumpiness.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, DOW. The second syllable has a short 'ih' sound, and the ending is a weak 'nuss'.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It describes a lack of style or charm, and calling a person's look 'dowdiness' can sound harsh.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this noun mainly in fashion, design, and media writing, or when giving a critical description of a look or style. In everyday talk, people more often say 'frumpy' or 'dowdy' as adjectives. Using the noun about a friend's outfit can sound critical, so choose your words carefully.

distinctions.note: Frumpiness is more colloquial and focuses on old-fashioned or shapeless clothes. Dowdiness is slightly more formal and can describe style, design, or general dullness.
Drabness means a lack of color or interest in anything, not only clothing. Dowdiness refers specifically to an unfashionable or unflattering appearance.
Plainness means simply without decoration, which is not necessarily unattractive. Dowdiness implies that the plainness looks unfashionable.

examples.everyday: Honestly, her cardigan had a certain dowdiness that her friends kept teasing her about.
examples.professional: The brand refresh aimed to move the store away from the dowdiness of its old catalog photos.
examples.analytical: Critics read the film's visual dowdiness as a deliberate rejection of consumer glamor.

nuance.analogy: Like a worn cardigan: comfortable and familiar, but nobody would call it stylish.
nuance.etymology: From dowdy plus the noun suffix -ness; the origin of dowdy is uncertain.
common_mistakes: Stressing the last syllable, as in dow-dih-NESS; the stress stays on DOW.
Keeping the y in the spelling as 'dowdyness'; the y changes to i before -ness.

senses.definition: A short, unintentional nap, an instance of dozing off.
senses.example: My afternoon doze off at the desk lasted only ten minutes, but it helped.

senses.definition: To fall asleep unintentionally.

core.definition: To fall asleep without intending to, usually for a short time.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on OFF, the particle, and the z in doze is voiced. In fast speech the two words link into something close to 'DOHZ-AWF'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral, with a slight note of embarrassment when the speaker is apologizing.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say doze off for sleeping unintentionally, such as during a long drive or a boring lecture, and it is a friendly everyday phrase. It can sound a bit self-deprecating, as in 'Sorry, I dozed off.' Use fall asleep when you mean going to sleep on purpose. A natural reply is 'No worries, it happens' or 'Me too, that meeting was long.'

distinctions.note: Fall asleep is neutral and can be planned or accidental, while doze off stresses sleeping unintentionally.
Pass out means to lose consciousness, often from illness or drinking, which is far more serious than dozing off.

collocations: doze off in front of the TV

examples.everyday: We were watching the movie and I totally dozed off on the couch.
examples.professional: I dozed off after the vendor's long slide deck, so I missed the pricing section.
examples.analytical: Many people doze off during dull reading, but researchers note that the lapse often follows a hard day rather than the content itself.

nuance.analogy: Dozing off is like a computer going into sleep mode on its own, without anyone sending a shutdown command.
nuance.etymology: Combines doze with the particle off, meaning away or into a state.
common_mistakes: Saying doze off to sleep, which is redundant; doze off already means fall asleep.
Using doze off for a planned nap, because it implies you did not mean to sleep.

senses.definition: To procrastinate, put off; to dawdle, avoid, or make progress slowly and reluctantly.
senses.example: I have been dragging my feet about filing my taxes.

senses.definition: To intentionally stall, to delay, to obstruct.
senses.example: The city council kept dragging its feet on the new bridge permit.

core.definition: To act slowly or reluctantly on something you should do, often putting it off or delaying progress on purpose.

pronunciation.tip: In this phrase, one's is reduced to a quick 'wunz', with the s pronounced as z. Link the words smoothly so that drag-wunz flows together, and stress feet most strongly.

nuance.connotation: Negative, because it suggests reluctance, delay, or lack of effort.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this idiom in work, politics, and family life to say that someone is moving too slowly or avoiding a task. It can sound critical, so it is often used when speaking about a third person rather than directly to someone. A natural reply when someone accuses you of this is, Sorry, I'll get on it right now.

distinctions.note: Procrastinate is more formal and suggests putting off tasks in general, while drag one's feet suggests reluctance or deliberate slowness.
Stall means to delay on purpose or to stop progress, and it can be more active than drag one's feet.

collocations: drag your feet on the contract

examples.everyday: Come on, stop dragging your feet, or we're going to miss the start of the movie.
examples.professional: The vendor has been dragging its feet on API access, so our launch date is stuck until legal signs off.
examples.analytical: Legislators who drag their feet on regulation often do so not from ignorance but from a strategic reluctance to impose costs before the next election.

nuance.analogy: It is like someone climbing the stairs in heavy boots on the way to a chore, every step slow and reluctant.
common_mistakes: Using the singular foot, as in 'drag your foot', which is not the standard idiom.
Using it to mean rushing or moving fast, which is the opposite of the meaning.

drag-one's-feet.etymology: From the idea of walking while dragging one's feet along the ground, either from lack of enthusiasm or to intentionally slow down movement.

senses.definition: To adapt a literary work so that it can be performed in the theater, or on radio or television.
senses.example: The network hired a writer to dramatize the memoir for a three-part television miniseries.

senses.definition: To present something in a dramatic or melodramatic manner.
senses.example: Please stop dramatizing every minor inconvenience; the printer jam isn't a catastrophe.

core.definition: To present something in an exaggerated, emotional way, or to adapt a story into a play, film, or show.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the first syllable, DRAM. The American a in this word is the short a sound, not the 'ah' sound of cot, so say DRAM rather than 'DRAH-muh.'

nuance.connotation: Negative when it means exaggerating; neutral when it means adapting a story for performance.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say 'Don't dramatize it' to tell someone to calm down and stop exaggerating. In a neutral sense, 'The novel was dramatized for TV' is common. Using it for a person's behavior can sound critical, so choose your tone carefully.

distinctions.note: Exaggerate means to make something seem larger than it is; dramatize means to present it with more emotion or theatrical effect.
Adapt is the general term for changing a work for a new medium; dramatize specifically means turning it into a play or dramatic production.

examples.everyday: Stop dramatizing it, the car just needs a new tire.
examples.professional: The team dramatized the customer complaint in the presentation to make the problem feel urgent.
examples.analytical: The historian warns that the filmmakers dramatized events so heavily that the public now mistakes fiction for documentary record.

nuance.analogy: Like a chef who turns a plain recipe into a restaurant-style show, dramatizing gives the story more energy and emotion.
nuance.etymology: From dramatic, from Greek dramatikos, plus the verb suffix -ize.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the first vowel as 'ah' as in cot, which sounds British or non-native.
Using dramatize to mean simply describing something; it implies emotion or exaggeration.

senses.definition: To visit informally and spontaneously.
senses.example: I dropped by on Thursday, but you were out.

core.definition: To visit someone briefly and informally, usually without a formal invitation or appointment.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on DROP, and the final by is pronounced like bye. In quick speech the two words run together.

nuance.connotation: Positive and friendly; it suggests a casual, warm visit.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say drop by most often with a person or a place, usually with an invitation such as Feel free to drop by. It is friendly and casual, used among neighbors, friends and coworkers. A natural reply is Sure, come by anytime or I'd love that. Stop by means nearly the same thing and is equally common.

distinctions.note: Nearly the same; stop by is slightly more common and can also describe a short stop on the way somewhere.
Drop in is more spontaneous and sometimes implies arriving with no warning at all.

collocations: drop by on the way home

examples.everyday: Hey, I was in the neighborhood, so I thought I'd drop by and say hi.
examples.professional: I'll drop by your desk after the stand-up to go over the dashboard numbers.
examples.analytical: The phrase drop by suggests a visit that is brief and unplanned, which changes what the host is expected to do.

nuance.analogy: It is like a quick stop at a friend's house on your walk home, with no set plan.
nuance.etymology: From drop, meaning to let fall or come down, plus by, meaning near or past; the visiting sense developed later.
common_mistakes: Saying drop to or drop at a person's house instead of drop by.
Using drop by for a formal visit; it sounds too casual for an official meeting.

conversation.text: Feel free to drop by anytime this weekend.
I dropped by the office to pick up my laptop.
Feel free to drop by anytime. We're usually home in the evenings.
My sister dropped by with some soup when I was sick.
I'll drop by your office later with those papers you need.

senses.definition: Of or relating to dualism.

core.definition: Relating to dualism, the view that reality or the mind consists of two fundamental, opposed principles or substances, such as mind and matter.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on LIS, the same syllable as in dualist, with a lighter secondary stress on DOO. Non-native speakers often stress the first syllable or say the middle as two separate vowels; in fast speech the middle syllable is quick and reduced.

nuance.connotation: Neutral in philosophy and theology, where it describes a position. Used about a person's outlook, it is mildly critical, suggesting that they see the world in sharp, either-or oppositions.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use dualistic mainly in academic, philosophical, religious and critical writing, and occasionally in serious conversation about worldviews. In casual speech people more often say black-and-white or either-or to make the same point. Calling someone's thinking dualistic is an intellectual criticism that can sound condescending if it is not explained.

distinctions.note: Dichotomous means divided into two exclusive parts, and it can describe any classification; dualistic specifically refers to a theory that reality rests on two fundamental principles.
Binary is a technical term in computing and statistics for a system with two states; dualistic is a philosophical term for a worldview, and it is rarely used for data.

collocations: dualistic view of mind and body

examples.everyday: My brother sees every decision as either right or wrong, which is pretty dualistic.
examples.professional: Our team's dualistic framing of data quality versus model speed is slowing down the roadmap.
examples.analytical: Descartes's dualistic account of mind and body leaves unexplained how an immaterial mind interacts with the physical brain.

nuance.analogy: A dualistic view is like a light switch that is only ever fully on or fully off, with no dimmer in between.
nuance.etymology: From dualism, from Latin dualis meaning consisting of two, from duo meaning two, plus the suffix -istic.
common_mistakes: Stressing the first syllable as in DOO-uh-liz-tik instead of stressing LIS.
Using dualistic to mean simply having two parts; it implies two opposed fundamental principles, not just any pair.
Confusing dualistic with dualism's noun form in sentences where an adjective is needed, as in saying a dualism view instead of a dualistic view.

senses.definition: Bewildering; astonishing.

core.definition: Astonishing or baffling to such a degree that it leaves people unable to react or respond.

pronunciation.tip: Stress is on the first syllable, DUHM, and the b is silent. The 'ou' is a diphthong that sounds like 'ow' in 'cow'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to strong; it describes something astonishing or absurd, and it is often negative when the surprise is unpleasant.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use dumbfounding to describe a result, mistake or fact that is hard to believe, such as 'a dumbfounding lack of planning'. It is less common than dumbfounded and is used mainly to describe things, not people. In casual talk, people more often say 'unbelievable' or 'mind-blowing'. A natural reply is 'Right? I still can't believe it.'

distinctions.note: Astonishing is a general word for something very surprising or impressive; dumbfounding suggests the surprise is so great that it leaves you speechless.
Baffling emphasizes confusion rather than shock; dumbfounding combines confusion with astonishment.

examples.everyday: It's dumbfounding that the coffee shop still doesn't take cards these days.
examples.professional: The dataset had a dumbfounding number of duplicate rows, which pointed to a broken import job.
examples.analytical: The dumbfounding circularity of his argument, in which the conclusion is simply restated as its premise, is easy to miss on a first reading.

nuance.analogy: Like a magic trick you still can't explain after watching it twice.
nuance.etymology: Present participle of 'dumbfound', from 'dumb' (unable to speak) and 'founder' (to collapse).
common_mistakes: Using it to describe a person who is shocked; use 'dumbfounded' for people and 'dumbfounding' for things.
Pronouncing the b in 'dumb'.
Confusing it with 'confounding', which means confusing or puzzling, without the element of astonishment.

senses.definition: Characteristic of a duopoly.

core.definition: Relating to or characteristic of a market controlled by two sellers.

pronunciation.tip: The primary stress falls on LIS, with a lighter stress on the first syllable. The middle syllables are weak, and the -ic ending is short, not stressed.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; a precise term used in economic analysis, sometimes with a mildly critical tone.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use duopolistic mostly in economics, business journalism and policy writing. In conversation they would more likely say two companies dominate the market. It can imply that the two firms behave in a coordinated or uncompetitive way, so use it carefully.

distinctions.note: Oligopolistic describes markets with a few sellers, while duopolistic specifies exactly two.
Monopolistic describes a market with one dominant seller, so it has a different structure.

examples.everyday: Those two grocery chains have a pretty duopolistic setup in our county, so they hardly compete on price.
examples.professional: The memo argues that our duopolistic pricing pattern has held for years because neither firm wants a price war.
examples.analytical: A duopolistic market can yield prices between competitive and monopoly levels, depending on how the two firms respond to each other.

nuance.analogy: Like two neighbors who share one driveway and quietly agree on who parks where.
nuance.etymology: From duopoly plus the adjective suffix -istic.
common_mistakes: Using duopolistic for a market with many sellers.
Stressing the -ic ending instead of LIS.

senses.definition: Relating to the earth or this world, as opposed to heaven or the heavens.
senses.example: The Garden of Earthly Delights is full of earthly joys alongside grotesqueries, monstrosities, and torture.

senses.definition: Used in negative contructions for emphasis.
senses.example: There is no earthly way, I mean no way on earth, that I will ever do that.

senses.definition: That which is of the earth or earthly; a terrestrial being.
senses.example: Among the gods and the earthlies, she was the only one who never lied.

senses.definition: In an earthly manner.

core.definition: Relating to this world and ordinary life, as opposed to heaven or spiritual things.

pronunciation.tip: Stress is on the first syllable. The 'th' is unvoiced, and 'thli' is said quickly, with no extra vowel between the 'th' and 'l'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral in most contexts. It can be positive when describing practical life, and negative when contrasted with spiritual values.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use earthly in both casual and formal speech, often to contrast the everyday world with heaven or spiritual things. In negative constructions like 'no earthly reason' it means 'any possible'. In casual speech people more often say 'no reason at all' or 'no way', so 'no earthly reason' sounds slightly old-fashioned and emphatic.

distinctions.note: Worldly often implies sophisticated or materialistic; earthly is more neutral and simply means relating to this life.
Mundane means dull or ordinary; earthly refers to the physical world, not boredom.

examples.everyday: My grandmother used to say she had no earthly idea how the new phone worked.
examples.professional: Our project budget covers only earthly costs, so we cannot add the cloud licenses.
examples.analytical: Augustine distinguishes the earthly city from the heavenly city, and this distinction shapes his philosophy of history.

nuance.analogy: Like a map of the streets we walk every day, as opposed to a map of the sky.
nuance.etymology: From Old English eorthlic, meaning of the earth.
common_mistakes: Adding a vowel, pronouncing it 'EARTH-uh-lee'.
Using it as a noun, where 'earthly' is a noun only in formal or theological writing.
nuance.biblical_note: The Greek word behind earthly is epigeios (ἐπίγειος), meaning of the earth or relating to this world. John 3:12 has Jesus say that if he tells Nicodemus earthly things and he does not believe, he will not believe heavenly things. Philippians 3:19 describes people whose minds are set on earthly things, in contrast with citizens of heaven. James 3:15 describes a false wisdom as earthly, unspiritual and devilish.

earthly.etymology: From Middle English *erthely*, *erthlich*, *ierðlich*, from Old English *eorþlīċ*, corresponding to *earth* + *ly*.

senses.definition: To make (something) long or longer, for example, by pulling or stretching; to make (something) elongated; to extend, to lengthen.
To become long or longer, for example, by being pulled or stretched; to become elongated.
senses.example: The shadows began to elongate as the sun sank behind the ridge.

senses.definition: Of a plant part: to grow long; also, to have a long and slender or tapering form.
senses.example: The seedlings elongate quickly under the grow lights when they get enough water.

senses.definition: Elongated, extended, lengthened; having a long and slender form.
senses.example: Painted turtles lay oval, elongate eggs.

core.definition: To make something longer or more stretched out, or to become longer and thinner; to lengthen or extend.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on LAWNG, the second syllable. The 'ng' is one sound, and the final syllable rhymes with 'gate'; do not add a hard 'g' after the 'n'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; a precise, descriptive word for physical or technical length.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use elongate mainly in science, engineering, and medicine, or in formal writing. In everyday speech they say 'stretch out,' 'make longer,' or 'lengthen.' Using it casually can sound stiff, but it is accurate and clear in technical writing.

distinctions.note: Lengthen is the everyday word for making something longer; elongate is more technical and often describes stretching or a long, slender shape.
Extend can mean to make longer or to continue in time or space; elongate focuses only on physical length or form.

examples.everyday: The tall cat tried to elongate itself under the couch, so I couldn't tell where it ended.
examples.professional: We need to elongate the timeout on the API so that slow requests don't fail during peak traffic.
examples.analytical: Darwin observed that over many generations the necks of certain animals elongate, and he argued that selection explains this change.

nuance.analogy: Like pulling on a piece of taffy until it stretches into a long rope, elongate describes a form that grows longer by being pulled out.
nuance.etymology: From Latin 'elongare', 'to remove far away', from 'e-' and 'longus', 'long'.
common_mistakes: Using 'elongate' for time periods in casual speech; in American English it usually refers to physical length.
Stressing the last syllable (ih-lawng-GAYT); the stress falls on the first syllable of the stressed pair, LAWNG.

senses.definition: Empirical.
Someone who is guided by empiricism; an empiricist.
senses.example: The early empiric trusted only what he observed at the bedside, not old textbooks.

senses.definition: Any unqualified or dishonest practitioner; a charlatan; a quack.
senses.example: The traveling empiric sold miracle tonics that did nothing but empty customers' wallets.

senses.definition: (historical) A member of a sect of ancient physicians who based their theories solely on experience.
senses.example: Galen criticized the empiric physicians of ancient Alexandria for ignoring anatomy and theory.
senses.label: historical

core.definition: Based on observation or experience rather than on theory; empirical. In medicine, it means a treatment started before a confirmed diagnosis.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the second syllable, PIH, not on the first. The r is pronounced in American speech, and the final -ic is 'ik'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and technical. As a noun meaning a quack, it is negative but archaic.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use empiric mainly in medicine, where empiric therapy or empiric antibiotics means treatment chosen from experience before lab results confirm it. In most other academic and business writing, empirical is the normal adjective. The noun empiric for a quack or a follower of empiricism is old-fashioned, so use empiricist for the philosophical sense.

distinctions.note: Empirical is the normal word for based on observation or evidence, while empiric is mostly limited to medicine and specialized use.
Theoretical describes ideas based on theory rather than observation, which is the opposite of empiric.
Anecdotal refers to evidence based on personal stories, which is weaker than systematic empirical or empiric observation.

examples.everyday: My doctor said they'd start me on an antibiotic right away as an empiric choice while we wait for the lab results.
examples.professional: Our data team takes an empiric approach, testing models against holdout data instead of trusting the theory alone.
examples.analytical: Hume's critique of induction challenges the claim that past empiric observations alone justify belief about the future.

nuance.analogy: Like tasting the soup before you read the recipe: you rely on what you actually experience.
nuance.etymology: From Greek empeirikos, 'experienced', from empeiria, 'experience'.
common_mistakes: Using empiric in general academic writing where empirical is the standard adjective.
Using the old noun meaning quack in modern conversation, where it will confuse listeners.

empiric.etymology: Latin *empiricus*, from Ancient Greek *ἐμπειρῐκός* (“experienced”), from *ἐμπειρία* (“experience, mere experience or practice without knowledge, especially in medicine, empiricism”), from *ἔμπειρος* (“experienced or practised in”), from *ἐν* (“in”) +…

senses.definition: An architecture in which an encoder turns the input into a representation and a decoder produces the output from it.
senses.example: We fine-tuned an encoder-decoder model to translate customer emails into structured summaries.

core.definition: A neural network design in which an encoder converts the input into a representation and a decoder generates the output from that representation.

pronunciation.tip: Both words stress the second syllable, KOH. In 'decoder' the first syllable is a short, reduced vowel, not 'dee'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it is a precise technical term used in research and engineering.
nuance.usage_note: Machine learning engineers and researchers say this term in papers, design reviews and talks about translation or summarization. Teams often shorten it to 'seq2seq' for sequence-to-sequence models. In a job interview, use the full term and explain what each part does.

distinctions.note: An autoencoder rebuilds its own input, while an encoder-decoder maps one sequence to a different output, such as a translation.
A transformer is an architecture that can be built as an encoder-decoder, but it can also be encoder-only or decoder-only.

examples.everyday: My cousin works on speech software, and she says their system is built as an encoder-decoder.
examples.professional: We chose an encoder-decoder architecture for the summarization model because the output length differs from the input length.
examples.analytical: An encoder-decoder separates reading the input from producing the output, which makes the bottleneck between the two stages a central design question.

nuance.analogy: Like a reader who takes notes on a book and a writer who produces a new text from those notes alone, the encoder reads and the decoder writes.
nuance.etymology: A compound of 'encoder' and 'decoder', from 'encode' and 'decode'.
common_mistakes: Dropping the hyphen in formal documents and writing 'encoder decoder' as two separate nouns.
Stressing the second word on its first syllable, as in 'DEE-kohd-er'.

conversation.text: The original transformer was an encoder-decoder model built for machine translation.
An encoder-decoder setup suits tasks where input and output are clearly separate, like translation.

senses.definition: The study of the endocrine glands of the human body, the hormones produced by them, and their related disorders.

core.definition: The branch of medicine that studies hormones, the glands that produce them, and disorders caused by hormone imbalances.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the NAH syllable, the third one. Begin with en, not END-oh, and reduce the middle syllables to light vowels.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and technical. It is used in medical education, research and clinical practice.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use endocrinology mainly in medical schools, hospitals and research, often in phrases like 'a fellowship in endocrinology.' People outside medicine usually talk about hormone problems or thyroid issues rather than the field itself. Clinics often list it as a department name.

distinctions.note: Endocrinology is the field of study; endocrine is the adjective describing glands or systems.
Pharmacology studies how drugs act in the body, while endocrinology focuses on hormones and their glands.

examples.everyday: My cousin is studying endocrinology because she wants to help people manage diabetes.
examples.professional: The endocrinology team wants the lab to add a cortisol test to the intake panel.
examples.analytical: Modern endocrinology treats hormones as parts of regulatory feedback loops rather than as isolated chemical messengers.

nuance.analogy: Like the body's postal service: hormones are the letters, and endocrinology studies who sends them, how they travel and what happens when deliveries go wrong.
nuance.etymology: From endocrine plus the suffix -ology, from Greek logos (study).
common_mistakes: Putting the stress on the wrong syllable, such as en-DOH-kruh-NAHL-uh-jee.
Confusing the field, endocrinology, with the doctor, endocrinologist.

senses.definition: To make more lively, cheerful or interesting.
senses.example: The game was much enlivened when both teams scored within five minutes of each other.

core.definition: To make something more lively, cheerful, or interesting, such as a party, a meeting or a dull room.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on LIVE, and the vowel is the diphthong /aɪ/, like the verb 'live' or 'alive', not the short 'i' of 'live' in 'give'. The final -en is weak, so the word ends in a soft 'vuhn'.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It describes making something more fun or interesting.
nuance.usage_note: In casual American speech people more often say 'liven up' or 'liven things up', as in 'Let's liven up this party'. 'Enliven' sounds a bit more formal or writerly, and it appears often in reviews, speeches and essays. It is used both for people and for things, such as a room, a meeting or a story.

distinctions.note: 'Liven up' is the more informal, common phrasal verb in speech. 'Enliven' is the more formal, one-word form.
'Invigorate' suggests restoring physical strength or energy. 'Enliven' suggests adding interest, cheer or fun.
'Animate' means to give life or movement, and it is often used for images or for physical motion. 'Enliven' is about adding fun or interest.

examples.everyday: A few jokes from my uncle really enlivened the dinner conversation.
examples.professional: Adding a few visuals will enliven the presentation and keep people from checking their phones.
examples.analytical: Dickens uses comic dialogue to enliven scenes that otherwise carry a grim argument about social neglect.

nuance.analogy: Like a squeeze of lemon on a flat soda that suddenly tastes bright again.
nuance.etymology: From en- + liven, from 'lively', from Old English lifian, 'to live'.
common_mistakes: Saying 'enliven up', which is redundant; say 'enliven' or 'liven up'.
Pronouncing the vowel as short 'i' (in-LIV-en) instead of the long 'eye' sound of 'live'.

senses.definition: To make sure or certain of something (usually some future event or condition).
senses.example: I use an alarm clock to ensure that I get up on time.

core.definition: To make certain that something will happen or be true, by taking the necessary steps in advance.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the second syllable, 'shur,' and make the first syllable very weak, like 'in.' Keep the r sound clear, and do not confuse it with 'insure,' which is pronounced the same but means something different.

nuance.connotation: Positive, implying careful planning and responsibility
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'ensure' often in workplace emails, instructions, and policies, as in 'please ensure the form is signed.' In casual talk, 'make sure' is more natural. Use 'ensure that' followed by a clause, not 'ensure to.'

distinctions.note: Insure is used for insurance contracts against loss, while ensure means to make sure that something happens.
Assure is used for telling someone something to comfort them, while ensure refers to taking action to guarantee an outcome.
Guarantee is stronger and often carries a promise or legal commitment, while ensure refers more to planned steps.

examples.everyday: Can you ensure the kids get to bed before nine, since we have an early flight?
examples.professional: Please ensure the data pipeline is validated before we deploy the new model on Friday.
examples.analytical: A just legal system must ensure that the rights of minorities are protected even when majorities vote against them.

nuance.analogy: To ensure something is like buckling a seat belt before the car moves, taking a sure step so that the outcome is protected.
nuance.etymology: From Anglo-French enseurer, from en- (make) plus seur (sure, certain), from Latin securus.
common_mistakes: Confusing 'ensure' with 'insure,' which is about insurance policies.
Writing 'ensure to' instead of 'ensure that' before a clause.

ensure.etymology: From Middle English *ensuren*, from Anglo-Norman *enseurer*, from Old French *seur* (“sure”).

senses.definition: To make a definite or systematic statement of.
senses.example: The committee will enunciate its principles in a written statement next month.

senses.definition: To announce, proclaim.
senses.example: The mayor enunciated the new curfew to residents at a packed town meeting.

senses.definition: To articulate, pronounce.
senses.example: You must enunciate all the syllables.

senses.definition: To make sounds clearly.
senses.example: Enunciate when you speak.

core.definition: To pronounce words clearly and distinctly so that other people can understand them.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the first syllable of the stem, NUN, and the final -ate is pronounced 'ayt'. Learners often stress the last syllable or say 'ee-NUN-see-ate'.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It suggests careful, clear speech, and it is often praised in teachers, speakers and newscasters.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use enunciate mainly about speech, as in 'Please enunciate when you leave a voicemail.' In casual talk people more often say 'speak clearly' or 'say your words clearly.' A natural reply to a request is 'Sure, I'll slow down.'

distinctions.note: Pronounce means to produce a word's sounds; enunciate adds the idea of doing so clearly and distinctly.
Articulate can mean speaking well or expressing ideas clearly, while enunciate focuses on the sounds of speech.

examples.everyday: Could you enunciate a little more? I can't hear the street name over the traffic.
examples.professional: During the presentation, please enunciate the variable names so the transcription software captures them correctly.
examples.analytical: Rhetorical clarity depends partly on the speaker's ability to enunciate each claim so that the audience can follow the argument.

nuance.analogy: Like cleaning a window so the view through it is sharp rather than blurred.
nuance.etymology: From Latin enuntiare, to announce, from e- 'out' and nuntiare 'to report'.
common_mistakes: Confusing enunciate with annunciate, which means to announce or proclaim and is rare in everyday speech.
Dropping the final t, which should be a clear 'ayt' sound.

enunciate.etymology: From Latin *ēnuntiātus*, past participle of *ēnuntiō* (“to report, declare”), from *ē-* + *nūntiō* (“to report”).

senses.definition: In terms of, or by using, enzymes.
senses.example: The sugars were broken down enzymatically before the mixture was fermented into beer.

core.definition: By means of enzymes, or in a way that involves enzyme action.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on MAT, and the ending '-ically' is pronounced 'ik-lee', with no separate 'ih-kal' syllable. Keep the 'z' voiced and the 'y' like 'eye'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a scientific word used to describe how a process happens.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this adverb mainly in scientific papers, lab reports, and industry descriptions of food, cleaning, or biotech processes. Ordinary speakers rarely need it, since they would say 'with enzymes' or 'using enzymes'. It usually follows a verb or precedes an adjective.

distinctions.note: Chemically is broader and includes any chemical process, while enzymatically specifies that enzymes are the agents.
Biologically refers to living systems in general, while enzymatically names the specific protein catalysts involved.

examples.everyday: The cleaner breaks down the stain enzymatically, so you don't have to scrub as hard.
examples.professional: We modified the protein enzymatically to improve its stability in the buffer before the next trial.
examples.analytical: A living system is enzymatically organized, so its reactions depend on catalysts whose shape and location matter.

nuance.analogy: Like a team of specialized workers who each do one job on an assembly line, moving the product along quickly.
nuance.etymology: From enzymatic plus the adverb suffix -ally.
common_mistakes: Stressing the wrong syllable, as in en-ZY-mat-ik-lee; the stress belongs on MAT.
Using 'enzymatically' for any chemical process; the word specifically means by means of enzymes.

senses.definition: An allegiant of the Israelite tribal patriarch Ephraim, a member of the tribe purportedly descended from him, or an inhabitant of the Northern Kingdom of Israel (930–720 B.C.), in which the tribe of Ephraim was preëminent.
senses.example: The sermon described the Ephraimites as a proud tribe in the north of ancient Israel.

core.definition: A member of the tribe of Ephraim, one of the tribes of ancient Israel, or a person from the Northern Kingdom of Israel.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the first syllable, EE. The 'ph' is an 'f' sound, and the middle syllable 'fray' rhymes with 'day'. Do not say 'eff-ray-im-ite' with the stress on the last syllable.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a historical and biblical term without emotional charge.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use Ephraimite mainly in Bible study, history lessons or scholarly discussions of ancient Israel. In everyday church talk you would more likely say 'a man from Ephraim' or 'the tribe of Ephraim'. The term is historically specific and does not describe modern people, except as a rare figure of speech.

distinctions.note: A Manassite was a member of the tribe of Manasseh, Ephraim's brother; the two tribes are often named together in the Bible.
Israelite is the broader term for any descendant of Jacob or member of the nation, while Ephraimite is specific to one tribe.

examples.everyday: During our Bible study, the leader said the Ephraimites were a powerful tribe in the north.
examples.professional: The seminar slide listed the Ephraimite tribal boundaries alongside the territories of Judah and Benjamin.
examples.analytical: In Judges 12, the quarrel with the Ephraimites reveals rivalry between tribes that the narrative uses to show the fragility of Israel's unity.

nuance.analogy: An Ephraimite is like a member of a particular family within a large clan: part of the whole, yet with its own name and history.
nuance.etymology: From Hebrew Ephrayim, the name of Joseph's younger son, which Genesis 41:52 connects with being fruitful.
common_mistakes: Putting the stress on the last syllable (eff-ray-im-ITE); the stress belongs on the first syllable.
Pronouncing the 'ph' as a 'p'; it is an 'f' sound, as in 'Ephesus'.
nuance.biblical_note: Ephraimite refers to a member of the tribe of Ephraim, named after Joseph's younger son. The Hebrew name Ephrayim is linked in Genesis 41:52 to being fruitful. Key passages: Genesis 41:52 records Joseph naming his second son Ephraim because God made him fruitful in the land of his affliction. Genesis 48:14-20 tells how Jacob crossed his hands to bless Ephraim above the older Manasseh. Judges 12:1-6 describes a conflict between the Ephraimites and Jephthah, and a test using the word shibboleth that revealed who was an Ephraimite by their pronunciation.

ephraimite.etymology: An adaptation of the Latin *Ephraimītēs*, *Ephraimīta*, from the Ancient Greek *Ἐφραιμίτης*, from *Ἐφραίμ* + *ῑ́της*.

senses.definition: A widespread disease that affects many humans in a population.
An occurrence of a disease or disorder in a human population at a frequency higher than that expected in a given time period; an episode of outbreak and subsequent high prevalence.
senses.example: The flu epidemic filled the county hospital with patients during the winter of 2018.

senses.definition: A heightened occurrence of anything harmful.
senses.example: Officials warned of an epidemic of opioid overdoses in rural towns across the state.

senses.definition: The spreading of an idea or belief amongst a population.
senses.example: The misleading theory became an epidemic among students, spreading from one dorm to another.

senses.definition: Of, related to, or being an epidemic: a widespread outbreak of disease in humans.
senses.example: Health officials tracked the epidemic spread of measles through the county's unvaccinated neighborhoods.

senses.definition: Like an epidemic: widespread in a bad way.
senses.example: Epidemic hysteria occurred upon the incumbent’s reelection.

core.definition: A widespread outbreak of a disease that affects many people in a community or region at the same time.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the syllable -dem-. Americans reduce the middle vowels, so the second and third syllables sound like 'ih' and 'ik'.

nuance.connotation: Negative
nuance.usage_note: Americans use epidemic for disease outbreaks and, more loosely, for any widespread harmful problem, such as an epidemic of loneliness or opioid misuse. In health news, people distinguish epidemic from pandemic, which covers a wider geographic area. Speaking casually, you can say 'an epidemic of' before a problem to describe its spread.

distinctions.note: A pandemic spreads across many countries or continents; an epidemic is confined to a community or region, though it can be large.
An outbreak is a sudden appearance of disease in a place; an epidemic is a larger, sustained spread that exceeds the expected rate.

examples.everyday: My neighbor said there's an epidemic of colds at her kids' school, so everyone is staying home this week.
examples.professional: Our data dashboard flagged an epidemic-level spike in customer complaints after the software update.
examples.analytical: The author argues that the so-called epidemic of loneliness is partly a measurement artifact, since prevalence depends on how the condition is defined.

nuance.analogy: An epidemic is like a grass fire: it starts in one patch, but the wind of contact carries it across the field faster than anyone expected.
nuance.etymology: From Greek epidēmios, 'among the people', from epi ('among') and dēmos ('people').
common_mistakes: Using epidemic as a countable noun without an article in phrases like 'an epidemic of' versus 'epidemic of'.
Confusing epidemic with pandemic, which Americans use for a much wider spread.

epidemic.etymology: From French *épidémique*, from *épidémie*, from Medieval Latin *epidēmia*, reanalysis of plural Late Latin *epidēmia*, from Ancient Greek *ἐπιδήμιος*, from *ἐπί* (“upon”) + *δῆμος* (“people”).

senses.definition: Constituting an epoch; opening a new era; introducing new conceptions or a new method in the treatment of a subject; highly novel and influential.
senses.example: Her epoch-making paper on statistical learning changed how our entire field approaches prediction.

core.definition: Marking the start of a new era; so original or influential that it changes how something is done or understood.

pronunciation.tip: Stress EP first and MAY second. The ch in epoch is pronounced like a /k/ sound, not like the ch in church, so say EP-uk, and the -ing is a short, quick ending.

nuance.connotation: Positive; it praises something as a major turning point, though it can sound exaggerated when used for small events.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use epoch-making in news, business, science and history to describe a truly major change, such as a breakthrough invention or landmark decision. In everyday talk it can be used with some humor for something that felt huge to you personally. Using it for minor changes sounds overblown, so save it for things that really changed a field.

distinctions.note: Groundbreaking stresses that something is new and pioneering, while epoch-making emphasizes that it marks a turning point in history.
Historic describes something important that happened or will be remembered, while epoch-making highlights that it started a new era in a field.

examples.everyday: Getting my first GPS on a road trip was epoch-making for me, since I never got lost again after that.
examples.professional: The transformer architecture paper was epoch-making for our field, and our whole model stack now builds on it.
examples.analytical: Darwin's On the Origin of Species was an epoch-making work, changing how biologists understood the history of life.

nuance.analogy: An epoch-making change is like a river changing its course: after it happens, the whole landscape looks different.
nuance.etymology: Epoch comes from Greek epokhē 'a stopping point or fixed point in time', from epekhein 'to hold back'.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing epoch as EE-pock or with a ch sound; say EP-uk.
Using epoch-making for small everyday changes, which sounds exaggerated to Americans.

senses.definition: The sale of a person's possessions after their death, normally formalized by the executor of the estate.
senses.example: After her father died, the family held an estate sale to sell his furniture, tools, and old records.

core.definition: A public sale of a dead person's household belongings, usually run by the executor or a professional company to clear out a home.

pronunciation.tip: As a compound noun, the first word 'ESTATE' carries the main stress, and 'sale' is lighter. Don't stress both words equally, as in 'ih-STAYT SAYL'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to slightly sad at first, but Americans often treat estate sales as a chance to find bargains and antiques.
nuance.usage_note: Estate sales are common in American neighborhoods and are advertised online and in local papers, often with 'Everything Must Go' signs. People go early to get the best items, and prices often drop on later days. Saying 'I'm going to an estate sale Saturday' is a normal, friendly remark.

distinctions.note: A garage sale is held by living owners who want to clear out their own items; an estate sale involves the belongings of someone who has died.
An auction has bidding for each item; an estate sale usually has fixed prices, though some use auctions.
A yard sale is informal and small-scale; an estate sale is typically larger, with the whole house's contents on display.

examples.everyday: Let's check out that estate sale on Maple Street Saturday morning before the good stuff is gone.
examples.professional: The firm handles estate sales for families who need the house cleared before listing it.
examples.analytical: An estate sale turns a person's private belongings into market goods, so its prices reflect both sentiment and the executor's duty to heirs.

nuance.analogy: An estate sale is like a museum exhibit in reverse: the whole life of a household is laid out for strangers to buy.
nuance.etymology: Compound of 'estate' (from Old French estat) and 'sale' (from Old Norse sala).
common_mistakes: Thinking an estate sale sells the house; it sells the contents, while the property is sold separately.
Assuming it is always cheap; popular estate sales can have high prices on collectibles.

senses.definition: (archaic) Ethiopian.
senses.label: archaic

core.definition: Relating to Ge'ez, the classical language of Ethiopia, or to the script used to write Ge'ez, Amharic, and related languages.

pronunciation.tip: Use four syllables and place the main stress on the third, AH. The th is voiceless, and the first vowel is a long ee.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a precise term in scholarship and religious studies, not a casual word.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use Ethiopic in everyday speech. In academic and church settings, it refers to the language, script, or manuscripts of the Ethiopian tradition. For people or nationality, say Ethiopian; the older use of Ethiopic to mean Ethiopian sounds archaic.

distinctions.note: Ethiopian is the normal word for people, nationality, and things from Ethiopia; Ethiopic is specialized for the language, script, or classical tradition.
Ge'ez is the name of the classical language; Ethiopic often describes the writing system used for it.
Amharic is a modern language written in the Ethiopic script, so the script can be called Ethiopic even when the text is in Amharic.

examples.everyday: The coffee bag had Ethiopic letters on it, so I asked the barista what they said.
examples.professional: The localization team needs full Ethiopic script support for the Amharic version of the app.
examples.analytical: Ethiopic manuscripts preserve Ge'ez texts that Western scholars only began editing systematically in the nineteenth century.

nuance.analogy: Like the Latin alphabet, which is used for many languages, Ethiopic is a writing system shared by several languages.
nuance.etymology: From Latin Aethiopicus, from Greek Aithiopikos, from Aithiops, 'burnt-faced,' the ancient Greek name for peoples south of Egypt.
common_mistakes: Using Ethiopic to describe a person, which sounds archaic; say Ethiopian instead.
Stressing the first or second syllable instead of the AH in the third position.
Confusing Ethiopic, the script or language, with Ethiopian, the nationality.
nuance.biblical_note: The word Ethiopic does not appear in Scripture. The Greek word Aithiops, translated Ethiopian, renders the Hebrew Kush or Cush, the region south of Egypt. Acts 8:26-40 tells of Philip meeting and baptizing an Ethiopian court official, and Jeremiah 38:7 names Ebed-melech the Ethiopian, a court official who helps rescue the prophet Jeremiah.

senses.definition: Conveying praise or admiration, as in a eulogy.

core.definition: Expressing high praise, especially in a formal speech or piece of writing; full of warm admiration.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on JIS, the third syllable of the word. Many learners put the stress on the first syllable or pronounce the middle syllable as 'loh', so keep the 'uh' vowel.

nuance.connotation: Positive, but it can suggest praise that is excessive or insincere, depending on context.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use eulogistic mainly in book reviews, obituaries, speeches and literary criticism. In casual conversation people would say 'glowing', 'over-the-top' or 'really nice'. The word can carry a slight suggestion that the praise is too strong.

distinctions.note: Laudatory is more neutral and formal, meaning simply praising, while eulogistic suggests warmer and more emotional praise.
Complimentary is an everyday word for kind comments, whereas eulogistic is much stronger and usually belongs in formal writing or speech.

examples.everyday: My sister gave me a eulogistic speech about my cooking, and I'm still not sure I deserved all of it.
examples.professional: The vendor's proposal was full of eulogistic claims about its AI platform, but it included no benchmark results.
examples.analytical: The biography's eulogistic portrait of the general leaves out the evidence that complicates his military record.

nuance.analogy: A eulogistic review is like beautiful gift wrap: it looks wonderful, so you should check what is inside.
nuance.etymology: From eulogy, from Greek eulogia, 'praise', with the adjective suffix -istic.
common_mistakes: Using eulogistic for a simple compliment, which overstates the level of praise.
Stressing the first syllable instead of the middle one, which changes the rhythm of the word.

senses.definition: (archaic) Euphonious; pleasing to the ear.
senses.example: The old poet praised the euphonical flow of the verses read aloud at dusk.
senses.label: archaic

core.definition: Pleasant to the ear; having a smooth, agreeable sound. This is an old-fashioned word that most Americans no longer use.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the second syllable, FAH, and keep the final -al very short, like 'kul'. It is a longer version of euphonic, so use the same stress pattern.

nuance.connotation: Positive but dated. It sounds old-fashioned in modern American speech.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use euphonical today. You might see it in older books, poetry or antique dictionaries. In modern English, people use euphonious or euphonic instead, and the older form can sound stilted or pretentious.

distinctions.note: Euphonic is the standard modern adjective, while euphonical is an older variant that sounds dated.
Euphonious is the common modern word for pleasant sound, so it is the better choice in almost every situation.

examples.everyday: Grandpa said the old hymn was euphonical, a word nobody uses anymore.
examples.professional: The editor cut the archaic phrase, since euphonical reads as confusing to younger readers.
examples.analytical: The poet's euphonical diction recalls earlier Victorian verse, though modern critics usually prefer euphonious.

nuance.analogy: Like a vintage recording: lovely to hear, but the style is clearly from another era.
nuance.etymology: From euphony, from Greek euphōnia, plus the adjective suffix -ical.
common_mistakes: Using euphonical in modern prose, where it sounds old-fashioned and stiff.
Confusing it with euphoric, which describes a feeling of joy.

core.definition: A major river of Western Asia, flowing from Turkey through Syria and Iraq to the Persian Gulf; one of the rivers of Eden in Genesis.

pronunciation.tip: Stress FRAY, the second syllable. Americans pronounce the r clearly and end the name with a 'teez' sound, not 'tees' or 'tez'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a geographic and historical name, sometimes with biblical or historical associations.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use Euphrates mainly in religious, historical or news contexts about Iraq and Syria. In a Bible study a speaker would say it naturally with the Tigris, often as 'the Tigris and the Euphrates.' It is not a casual word.

distinctions.note: The Tigris is the other great river of Mesopotamia, flowing parallel to the Euphrates; they are often named together.
The Nile is in Egypt and flows north; the Euphrates is in Mesopotamia and flows toward the Persian Gulf.

examples.everyday: We visited Iraq and saw the Euphrates from the riverbank, which surprised me because it is so wide.
examples.professional: The climate report noted that drought is reducing water flow in the Euphrates basin.
examples.analytical: In Genesis, the Euphrates marks the boundary of the promised land, so its geography shapes the theology of inheritance.

nuance.analogy: Like a long artery of the ancient Near East, carrying life and history across the desert.
nuance.etymology: From Latin Euphrates, from Greek Euphratēs, from Old Persian Ufrātu, ultimately related to Hebrew Perath.
common_mistakes: Stressing the wrong syllable, saying 'yoo-FRAY-tuhs' with a final 's' sound instead of 'z.'
Writing 'Euphrates' with 'Eu' pronounced as 'o' instead of 'yoo.'
nuance.biblical_note: The Hebrew name is Perath (פְּרָת), a river of Eden and a boundary of the promised land. Genesis 2:14 names the Euphrates as the fourth river flowing from Eden. Genesis 15:18 describes the land promised to Abraham's descendants as extending from the river of Egypt to the great river Euphrates. Revelation 16:12 describes the sixth angel pouring out a bowl on the great river Euphrates, which is dried up to prepare a way for the kings of the east.

senses.definition: Pertaining to the doctrines or teachings of the Christian gospel or Christianity in general.
senses.example: Her evangelical sermon focused on grace, repentance, and the meaning of the Christian gospel.

senses.definition: Pertaining to the gospel(s) of the Christian New Testament.
Protestant; specifically Lutheran and Calvinist churches in continental Europe as well as their offshoots in North America.
senses.example: The Lutheran church in our town calls itself evangelical, reflecting its Protestant roots in Germany.

senses.definition: Pertaining to a movement in Protestant Christianity that stresses personal conversion and the authority of the Bible (evangelicalism).
Pertaining to Islamic groups that are dedicated to dawah and preaching the Quran and sunnah.
senses.example: The dawah group organized evangelical outreach, distributing Quran translations and teaching sunnah at the local mosque.

senses.definition: Zealously enthusiastic.
senses.example: He became evangelical about cold-brew coffee, pressing it on every colleague in the office.

senses.definition: A member of an evangelical church.
senses.example: Several evangelicals from the church volunteered at the food bank every Saturday morning.

senses.definition: An advocate of evangelicalism.
senses.example: The bishop was an outspoken evangelical who pushed the diocese to expand missions abroad.

core.definition: Of Protestant Christianity that stresses the authority of the Bible, personal conversion, and spreading the gospel.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the third syllable, JEL. Many learners stress the first syllable; the first syllable has secondary stress only. The g is 'j'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral in religious description; in politics, it can carry positive or negative associations depending on the speaker.
nuance.usage_note: In the US, 'evangelical' usually names a broad Protestant movement and its members, often tied to certain social or political views. Writers also use lowercase 'evangelical' to describe zealous advocacy, as in 'evangelical about running'. In Germany, 'evangelisch' means Protestant, but in American English it does not.

distinctions.note: Evangelistic describes efforts to spread the gospel; evangelical describes a movement or belief system.
Fundamentalists are a stricter subset of conservative Protestants; evangelicals are a broader group.
Mainline denominations are older, generally more liberal Protestant churches contrasted with evangelicals.

examples.everyday: I grew up in an evangelical church, but my wife is Catholic.
examples.professional: The survey compared turnout among evangelical and mainline Protestant voters.
examples.analytical: Bebbington defined evangelicalism by four marks: conversionism, activism, biblicism and crucicentrism.

nuance.etymology: From Greek euangelion, 'good news', via Latin evangelicus.
common_mistakes: Stressing the first syllable (EE-van-jel-ih-kul).
Using it as a synonym for any Christian or for 'Protestant' in general.
nuance.biblical_note: The root is Greek euangelion, 'good news', the gospel proclaimed by Jesus and the apostles (Mark 1:14-15; Romans 1:16). Paul calls the gospel the power of God for salvation to everyone who has faith.

traditions.view: Evangelicals emphasize Scripture alone, new birth, the atoning work of Christ and active sharing of the faith; they span Baptists, Pentecostals, nondenominational and many Reformed and Anglican believers. In Germany, 'evangelisch' means Lutheran or Reformed Protestant.

Catholics use 'evangelical' for gospel-centered mission, as in the 'evangelical counsels' of poverty, chastity and obedience, and 'new evangelization'. They do not normally call themselves Evangelicals in the Protestant sense.

Orthodox use it to mean 'of the Gospel', as in gospel readings, and generally see the Protestant evangelical movement as a separate tradition. The Orthodox share the call to witness but understand salvation within the Church's sacramental life.

evangelical.etymology: From *evangelic* + *-al*, from Old French *evangelique*, from Latin *evangelium*, from Ancient Greek *εὐαγγέλιον* (“good news”).

senses.definition: The quality of being evenhanded; fairness, impartiality.

core.definition: The quality of treating people or sides equally and fairly, without favoritism or bias.

pronunciation.tip: Stress EE, the first syllable, with a lighter secondary stress on HAND. Say the -ness ending as a weak nuhs. Do not pronounce hand as hend.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It praises fair and impartial treatment.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use evenhandedness for fairness in judging, mediating, or reporting, especially in politics, journalism, sports officiating, and management. It is more formal than fairness. In casual talk, people more often say 'she's fair' or 'he treats everyone the same.'

distinctions.note: Fairness is general and everyday. Evenhandedness specifically means treating opposing sides or people with equal consideration.
Impartiality is more abstract and formal, often used for judges and institutions. Evenhandedness emphasizes consistent day-to-day treatment.

examples.everyday: My kids know I try to treat them with evenhandedness, though it's hard when they both want the last cookie.
examples.professional: The moderator's evenhandedness kept the debate fair for both presenters.
examples.analytical: Evenhandedness in historical writing requires describing each party's claims in terms they would recognize as their own.

nuance.analogy: Like a balance scale with equal weights on both pans, so neither side tips it.
nuance.etymology: Even-handed meant evenly dealt, from the idea of distributing equally with the hand, using Old English hand.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing hand as hend.
Confusing the noun evenhandedness with the adverb evenhandedly, as in 'treated evenhanded' instead of 'treated evenhandedly.'

senses.definition: Predicted; forecast.

core.definition: Based on what is known or predicted before an outcome occurs, in advance of the event.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable of 'ante', and the 'ex' is 'eks', not 'egz'. Americans usually pronounce 'ante' as 'AN-tee', not 'AHN-tay'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a precise analytical term and carries no positive or negative judgment.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'ex ante' mostly in economics, statistics, finance, and policy discussions. In everyday talk, people say 'beforehand' or 'in advance' instead. In a meeting, you might hear 'the ex ante forecast' to distinguish a prediction from the actual result. A natural reply is simply to ask what the forecast assumed.
word_family: ante (noun, Latin root, rare in English)

distinctions.note: 'Ex ante' refers to predictions made before outcomes are known; 'ex post' refers to evaluations after the outcome is known.
'A priori' is used in philosophy and logic for knowledge independent of experience; 'ex ante' is used in economics and statistics for forecasts made in advance.

examples.everyday: I couldn't tell beforehand whether the plan would work, so my ex ante guess was just a guess.
examples.professional: The ex ante estimate of customer churn was 12 percent, but the actual figure came in lower.
examples.analytical: An ex ante evaluation of the policy considers what participants could reasonably expect before it began.

nuance.analogy: An ex ante forecast is like a weather report issued the night before, while an ex post report is the rainfall gauge the next morning.
nuance.etymology: From Latin ex 'from' and ante 'before'.
common_mistakes: Saying 'egz AN-tee' instead of 'eks AN-tee'.
Using 'ex ante' in casual speech where 'beforehand' is clearer.

related: ante (noun, Latin root, rare in English)

senses.definition: An increase in the severity of something (such as a disease)

core.definition: An increase in the severity of something, such as a disease, problem or conflict.

pronunciation.tip: This is a stress shift from exacerbate (ig-ZAS-er-bayt).

nuance.connotation: Negative. It always describes something getting worse.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use exacerbation mostly in medicine, news and formal writing, as in a flare-up or an exacerbation of symptoms. In conversation they usually say flare-up, getting worse or the problem came back. Use exacerbation when you want a precise, formal word for a sudden or added worsening.

distinctions.note: Deterioration is a gradual decline in quality or health, while exacerbation refers to a worsening of something already present, often a sudden flare-up.
Aggravation in everyday American speech means annoyance or trouble, as in what an aggravation; exacerbation is a formal word for the worsening of a condition.

examples.everyday: My doctor said the cough was an exacerbation of my asthma, probably from the cold weather.
examples.professional: The outage was an exacerbation of the database bottleneck we flagged in March.
examples.analytical: The reform was less a cure than an exacerbation of the structural inequalities it claimed to address.

nuance.analogy: Like a small leak in a boat that becomes a flood after a storm hits it: the exacerbation is the sudden worsening of a problem that was already there.
nuance.etymology: From Latin exacerbatio, from exacerbare, to make bitter or irritate, from ex- (intensive) and acerbus, bitter.
common_mistakes: Keeping the stress on ZAS as in exacerbate; the noun shifts the stress to BAY.
Using exacerbation as a verb; the verb is exacerbate.

exacerbation.etymology: From Middle English *exacerbacyoun*, from Latin *exacerbātiōnem*, from *exacerbāre* (“to provoke, make harsh”).

senses.definition: That exasperates, infuriates, annoys or irritates.

core.definition: Extremely irritating, frustrating or annoying in a way that tries your patience.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable of the stem, ZAS, not the -ate. The middle -er is a quick, r-colored vowel, and the final -ing is a nasal 'ing', not 'een'.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It describes something that wears down your patience, though it can be used playfully.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use exasperating in everyday speech about traffic, computers, slow service or stubborn people: 'This printer is exasperating.' It is stronger than 'annoying' and suggests repeated irritation. In formal writing, it can describe a difficult intellectual problem. A natural reply is 'I know, it's so frustrating.'

distinctions.note: Annoying is milder and more casual; exasperating describes irritation that exhausts your patience.
Frustrating focuses on being blocked from a goal; exasperating adds the sense of repeated irritation building up.

examples.everyday: Our printer is exasperating; it jams every single time I need it.
examples.professional: Dealing with the vendor's slow approvals has been exasperating, and the project is now two weeks behind.
examples.analytical: The skeptic's question is exasperating to believers, but it forces them to clarify what they mean by faith.

nuance.analogy: Like a drip from a faucet that never stops, wearing away your patience one drop at a time.
nuance.etymology: From Latin exasperare, 'to make rough, irritate', from ex- 'thoroughly' and asper 'rough'.
common_mistakes: Stressing the final syllable of the stem (ex-as-PER-ating) rather than the first, ZAS.
Confusing exasperating with exasperated; the first describes the thing causing the feeling, and the second describes the person who feels it.

senses.definition: An act or instance of cursing; a curse dictated by violent feelings of hatred; an imprecation; an expression of utter detestation.
senses.example: His letter was full of execration for the landlord who had evicted his family during the storm.

senses.definition: That which is execrated; a detested thing.
senses.example: Among the villagers, the new tax collector had become an execration, spat upon whenever he walked by.

core.definition: A bitter curse or angry denunciation; an expression of intense hatred for someone or something.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on '-kray-', and the middle 'uh' is reduced. The 'x' is pronounced 'ks', and the word is not confused with 'execution'.

nuance.connotation: Strongly negative; it expresses intense hatred and is rarely used lightly.
nuance.usage_note: Most Americans say 'curse', 'rant', or 'denunciation' instead. The word sounds dramatic or literary and appears mainly in essays, historical writing, or novels. Use it only when you want to emphasize the force of hatred.

distinctions.note: A curse is an ordinary word for an oath or wish of harm; execration is more formal, more intense, and more often written.
Condemnation is a judgment of wrongdoing; execration adds emotional hatred and loathing.

examples.everyday: The whole neighborhood heaped execration on the developer after the trees came down.
examples.professional: Public execration followed the outage, though the root cause was a bad config push, not one engineer.
examples.analytical: Dante reserves his most vivid execration for those who betray their kin, fixing them in the frozen depths.

nuance.analogy: Execration is a thunderclap of hatred: loud, sudden, and meant to be heard far away.
nuance.etymology: From Latin exsecratio, from exsecrari 'to curse', from ex- 'out' plus sacer 'sacred'.
common_mistakes: Confusing it with 'execution' because the first syllables sound similar.
Using it for mild disapproval; it signals intense hatred.

senses.definition: The state or characteristic of being exorbitant.
senses.example: Investors were stunned by the exorbitance of the new CEO's compensation package.

senses.definition: A large excess.

core.definition: The quality of being much too high or excessive, especially in prices, demands or spending.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on ZOR, and the last syllable is a weak, reduced vowel. Do not add an extra syllable at the end.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It implies that something is far beyond what is fair or reasonable.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use exorbitance in writing, news and formal complaints, usually about costs or demands. In everyday speech, people more often say the prices are crazy or way too much. It is a strong word, so use it when you want to sound precise and critical.

distinctions.note: Excess is a general word for too much of something. Exorbitance adds the idea that the amount is outrageous or unfair.
Extravagance describes spending too much on luxury. Exorbitance can describe prices or demands that are unreasonable, not just wasteful spending.

examples.everyday: The exorbitance of the wedding venue prices made us look for a park instead.
examples.professional: The vendor's exorbitance in its renewal quote forced us to renegotiate the contract.
examples.analytical: The essay critiques the exorbitance of executive pay as a symptom of weak accountability.

nuance.analogy: Exorbitance is like a thermostat stuck on maximum. The number is far past what anyone reasonable would set.
nuance.etymology: From Late Latin exorbitare, to go out of the track, from ex- (out) and orbita (track).
common_mistakes: Confusing exorbitance with exorbitant in a sentence, using the noun where an adjective is needed.
Using exorbitance for a small or moderate price difference, which is too strong.

senses.definition: Any exothermic compound.

core.definition: A chemical compound or substance that releases heat when it forms, reacts, or decomposes.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the first syllable, EK. The second syllable, soh, has a long o sound, and the final syllable has an r-colored vowel that ends in m.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it is a technical term that describes heat release without emotional tone.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use exotherm in chemistry, materials science, and engineering, usually when discussing reactions or industrial processes. In everyday speech people would say a substance that gives off heat. The word is the noun form of exothermic, so it appears mainly in technical reports and lab discussions.

distinctions.note: An endotherm is a substance or process that absorbs heat, while an exotherm releases heat.
Exothermic reaction names the whole process of releasing heat, while exotherm can refer to the compound or substance itself.

examples.everyday: Don't add water to that powder all at once, because it's an exotherm and can splatter when it heats up.
examples.professional: The curing resin is a strong exotherm, so we need to monitor the core temperature during the first hour.
examples.analytical: Under standard conditions the reaction gives an exotherm with a negative enthalpy change, which makes its heat release predictable.

nuance.analogy: An exotherm is like a space heater that gives off warmth into the room as soon as you turn it on, whereas an endotherm takes warmth from the room.
nuance.etymology: From exo- 'outside' and Greek thermos 'hot', 'heat'; the noun is formed from exothermic.
common_mistakes: Using exotherm to mean any warm object rather than something that releases heat through a chemical or physical change.
Confusing exotherm with exothermic, the adjective, in technical writing.
Putting the stress on the second syllable, saying ek-SOH-therm.

senses.definition: Very specific, clear, or detailed.
senses.example: I gave explicit instructions for him to stay here, but he followed me, anyway.

senses.definition: Containing material (e.g. language or film footage) that might be deemed offensive or graphic through clear and direct expressions.
senses.example: The film had several scenes including explicit language and sex.

senses.definition: The final few words of a text.
senses.example: Scholars read the explicit of the manuscript, which named the copyist and the year.

senses.definition: Used at the conclusion of a book to indicate the end.
senses.example: The novel ended with the word Explicit printed neatly beneath the final chapter.
