examples.analytical: A permutational argument shows that the total count depends only on the number of distinct orderings, not on the particular labels.

nuance.analogy: Like counting every way to shuffle a row of books on a shelf.
nuance.etymology: From Latin permutare, 'to change thoroughly', from per- 'through' and mutare 'to change'.
common_mistakes: Putting the stress on the first syllable (PUR-) instead of TAY.
Using it in everyday conversation where 'rearranged' or 'in a different order' sounds more natural.

core.definition: A priest in the Hebrew Bible, son of Eleazar and grandson of Aaron, known for his zeal against idolatry and his role in Israel's worship and leadership.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, FY, as in 'fine'. The middle and last syllables are reduced, so do not say 'fi-NEE-has'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a biblical proper name, though his story of zeal is often discussed seriously.
nuance.usage_note: This is the standard English spelling in the RSV and most modern American Bibles. In church or Bible study, you might say 'Phinehas, son of Eleazar' to identify him. Americans may also refer to him as the priest who acted zealously in Numbers 25.

distinctions.note: Phinees is the Douay-Rheims spelling of the same name; in American church settings, Phinehas is the usual form.

examples.everyday: During Bible study, our pastor mentioned Phinehas, the priest whose zeal in Numbers really surprised the group.
examples.professional: In the sermon outline, Phinehas illustrates zeal for holiness, though the passage must be read carefully in its covenant context.
examples.analytical: Psalm 106 recalls Phinehas's act as righteousness reckoned to him, linking his zeal to the covenant of perpetual priesthood.

nuance.analogy: Phinehas is like a sentinel at the gate of a camp, acting quickly to protect the community from what threatens it.
nuance.etymology: From Hebrew Pinchas; its meaning is uncertain.
common_mistakes: Stressing the middle syllable, as in 'fi-NEE-has'.
Confusing him with Phinees, which is a different spelling of the same name.
nuance.biblical_note: Hebrew Pinchas (uncertain meaning) is the name of the priest son of Eleazar and grandson of Aaron. In Numbers 25:7-13 he acts with zeal against Zimri and Cozbi, and God makes a covenant of perpetual priesthood with him. In 1 Samuel 4:11 his name recurs among the sons of Eli, Hophni and Phinehas, who die in battle, and in Judges 20:28 he ministers before the ark during the war with Benjamin.

senses.definition: To digitally edit or alter (a picture or photograph).
senses.example: She charged that the prosecutor had photoshopped the image to incriminate her.

senses.definition: A digitally altered image.
senses.example: I reckon the image is a photoshop.

core.definition: To digitally edit or alter a photograph, often to improve it or to change it in a misleading way.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the first syllable, FOH, and the second syllable is a weak toh. The last syllable is shop with the cot vowel, not shope. Keep the sh sound clear.

nuance.connotation: Neutral in design talk, but negative when it suggests deception, as in photoshopped to look thinner.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use photoshop as a verb in lowercase, often without capitals, even though it is a trademark of Adobe. People say photoshopped or photoshopping in casual conversation about social media, advertising, or dating profiles. To describe a fake image, say a photoshopped picture. Because the word can imply deception, it is safer to say edited when you mean ordinary corrections.

distinctions.note: Edit is the general word for changing a file or image, while photoshop specifically refers to the editing software or to changes made with it.
Retouch means to fix small flaws in a photo, while photoshop can mean much larger changes, including changes that are misleading.

examples.everyday: Those vacation photos look perfect, but I bet he photoshopped the sky.
examples.professional: Legal said we can't use the product image unless it shows the item as it really is, not photoshopped.
examples.analytical: When advertisers photoshop models, they set unrealistic standards, which raises ethical questions about body image.

nuance.analogy: Photoshopping a picture is like a tailor letting out a seam: a small fix can make a garment fit, but too much changes the outfit entirely.
nuance.etymology: From Photoshop, the Adobe image-editing software first released in 1990; the name combines photo with shop.
common_mistakes: Capitalizing the verb as Photoshop in every sentence, when many Americans use lowercase for the verb.
Using photoshop for any camera filter, when it specifically means editing with software.

photoshop.etymology: of Adobe Photoshop, a widely-used graphics editor.

senses.definition: A short written or spoken expression.
senses.example: I've made progress, but this is still, in Churchill's phrase, just "the end of the beginning."

senses.definition: A word or, more commonly, a group of words that functions as a single unit in the syntax of a sentence, always containing an expressed or implied head (the principal word or subgroup, with core importance) and often consisting of a head plus some other elaborating words.
A short individual motion forming part of a choreographed dance.
A small section of music in a larger piece.
To express (an action, thought or idea) by means of particular words.
senses.example: I wasn't sure how to phrase my condolences without sounding patronizing.

senses.definition: To perform (a passage) with a particular phrasing.
To divide into melodic phrases.

core.definition: A short expression, or a group of words that works as one unit in a sentence, such as 'a cup of coffee' or 'in the morning'.

pronunciation.tip: It rhymes with 'praise' and 'days', and the final s is voiced like a z, so don't say 'frayss'. The r is pronounced clearly, and the single stressed syllable carries the whole word.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; the word itself carries no emotional value.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use phrase in everyday talk for a short saying or expression, as in 'What's the phrase for that?' In grammar it names a group of words smaller than a clause. Calling something 'his favorite phrase' is a natural way to point out a saying someone repeats often.

distinctions.note: A sentence has a subject and a finite verb; a phrase does not, so 'the big red house' is a phrase, not a sentence.
A phrase can be literal, like 'cup of tea'; an idiom has a meaning that cannot be predicted from its words, like 'kick the bucket'.

examples.everyday: Hey, what's the phrase for 'good luck' in Spanish?
examples.professional: Let's avoid the phrase 'circle back' in the client deck; it sounds vague.
examples.analytical: A noun phrase contains a head noun and its modifiers, so its grammar differs from that of a full clause.

nuance.analogy: A phrase is like a small set of tools bundled together: several parts that work as one tool.
nuance.etymology: From Latin phrasis, from Greek phrasis, 'manner of speaking'.
common_mistakes: Using phrase for a single word; a phrase needs at least two words.
Confusing phrase with paraphrase, which means restating an idea in other words.

phrase.etymology: Late Latin *phrasis* (“diction”), from Ancient Greek *φράσις* (“manner of expression”), from *φράζω* (“to tell, express”).

senses.definition: A person whose occupation specializes in the science of physics, especially at a professional level.
senses.example: My cousin became a physicist after years of studying quantum mechanics at Caltech.

core.definition: A scientist who studies physics, the properties and interactions of matter, energy, space and time, often doing research or teaching.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, and the vowels in the middle are short ih sounds. Avoid saying fi-ZIS-ist, and do not stress the -ist ending.

nuance.connotation: Positive and respected; it suggests expertise and rigorous thinking.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say physicist for the scientist and physician for a medical doctor, so the two words must be kept apart. Describing someone as a physicist is a respectful way to talk about their work. In everyday talk you may hear theoretical physicist or particle physicist for more specialized research.

distinctions.note: A physicist studies the laws of matter and energy, while a physician is a medical doctor; the words sound similar, but their meanings are completely different.
A physicist usually studies the fundamental principles of nature, while an engineer applies physics and other sciences to design and build things.
An astronomer studies stars, planets and galaxies, while a physicist can study the same objects using physics; astronomy is a narrower field.

collocations: a physicist at the national lab

examples.everyday: My brother's a physicist, so he can explain why the sky is blue, though I still don't follow him.
examples.professional: The team includes two physicists who handle the sensor calibration and error analysis.
examples.analytical: A physicist's model of gravity claims to describe reality independently of any particular observer.

nuance.analogy: A physicist is to the universe what a cartographer is to land: each maps the rules that the terrain follows.
nuance.etymology: From physics, from Greek physikos, of nature, with the suffix -ist for a person who practices a field.
common_mistakes: Confusing physicist with physician, which is a doctor.
Stressing the second syllable, saying fi-ZIS-ist.
Using physicist to mean any science teacher; the word refers specifically to physics.

senses.definition: A public square, especially in Italian cities.
A veranda; a porch.
senses.example: We sat on the piazza in rocking chairs, sipping iced tea as the sun went down.

core.definition: A public square in an Italian town or city, usually lined with buildings, cafés and churches.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the second syllable, AT. The double z is pronounced as a ts sound, not a buzzing z, so avoid pee-AZ-uh. Americans often say the vowel with the short a of cat.

nuance.connotation: Positive; it evokes Italian city life, leisure and open public space.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use piazza mainly when talking about a square in Italy, such as the piazza in Florence or Piazza San Marco in Venice. For a town square in the United States, say square or plaza. The porch sense is old and dated in American English, so use porch or veranda instead.

distinctions.note: Plaza is the common American word for a paved public square, especially in Spanish-speaking areas or new developments, while piazza is specifically Italian.
Square is the general English word for any public open space in a town, while piazza sounds specifically European.
A veranda is a covered porch along a house; the porch sense of piazza is dated, so veranda or porch is the usual word.

examples.everyday: We had gelato in the piazza in Florence and watched the street performers until it got dark.
examples.professional: The hotel's marketing uses photos of an Italian piazza to make its courtyard look like a European square.
examples.analytical: The Italian piazza works as a civic stage where religious processions, commerce and political life meet in one open space.

nuance.analogy: A piazza is a town's living room: a shared open space where people gather, talk and watch one another.
nuance.etymology: From Italian piazza, from Latin platea (broad street), from Greek plateia.
common_mistakes: Using piazza for any town square in America, where square or plaza is more natural
Pronouncing the double z as a buzzing z, as in pee-AZ-uh

senses.definition: Go and get someone in your car.

core.definition: To drive to a place and collect someone so you can take them somewhere in your car.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on pick and up. Someone reduces to SUM-wun, and pick up links into pi-KUP when the object is a pronoun like me or him.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It describes a helpful, friendly act.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say pick someone up for driving to get a person, such as a friend, a child, or a coworker, and then taking them somewhere. You can say I'll pick you up at seven. A natural reply is Sounds good, or Thanks for picking me up. The phrase does not mean meeting someone romantically in casual talk, though it can have that meaning in some contexts.

distinctions.note: Pick up means to collect someone, while drop off means to take someone to a place and leave them there.
Meet is neutral about transportation, while pick up specifically involves collecting someone, often by car.

collocations: pick me up at the airport
I'll pick you up at seven
pick up the kids from school
pick her up at the station

examples.everyday: Can you pick me up at the airport around six? My flight is running a bit late.
examples.professional: I'll pick up our client from the lobby and bring them to the conference room before the review.
examples.analytical: Critics argue that the state should pick up those whom the market has dropped, which raises questions about responsibility and dependence.

nuance.analogy: Picking someone up is like collecting a package at the post office, except the package can talk and expects a ride.
common_mistakes: Saying pick up someone at the place without the object in the right position; the object goes between pick and up in the phrase.
Confusing pick someone up with drop someone off, which means the opposite action.

conversation.text: Can you pick me up from the airport on Friday?
School gets out at three, so I need to pick my son up.
She picked her mom up at the train station.

senses.definition: A light truck with an open cargo bed.

core.definition: A light truck with an open cargo bed behind the cab, used for hauling loads and driving on rough roads.

pronunciation.tip: Americans stress PICK in pickup, and the second word is also stressed, so the phrase has two strong beats. Note that pickup here has the vowel of cup, not the vowel of cop.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It names a common vehicle, and it can suggest work, rural life or practical use.
nuance.usage_note: Pickup truck is the standard American term, and Americans say it constantly. Shortened forms like pickup or truck are common in conversation. The word pickup alone can also mean a small truck or a shortened form of the phrase in a casual setting.

distinctions.note: In casual speech, pickup alone usually means a pickup truck, but it can also mean a ride picked up by someone or a small gathering.
A van is enclosed with a roof over the cargo area, while a pickup has an open bed.

collocations: park the pickup truck in the driveway

examples.everyday: I can give you a ride to the hardware store; I'll bring the pickup truck.
examples.professional: Our field crews use a half-ton pickup truck to haul equipment between job sites.
examples.analytical: The pickup truck has become a symbol of American utility and independence in both policy debates and popular culture.

nuance.analogy: A pickup truck is like a shoebox with the lid removed: the cab is the closed front, and the open bed is the exposed space in back.
nuance.etymology: From the verb pick up, meaning to collect or lift, because the bed was used to collect loads.
common_mistakes: Saying the vowel of cop in pickup; the first syllable of pickup uses the vowel of cup.
Calling it a lorry or utility truck, which are British or non-standard terms.

pickup-truck.etymology: but likely related to its intended use to *pick up* various supplies.

conversation.text: My neighbor has a pickup truck, so he helped us move the couch.
Can I borrow your pickup truck this weekend to haul some firewood?
A pickup truck was blocking the driveway, so we had to wait.

senses.definition: Having two or more colors, especially black and white.
Decorated or colored in blotches.
senses.example: The pied cattle in the field looked like patches of black and white paint.

core.definition: Marked with irregular patches of two or more colors, especially black and white.

pronunciation.tip: Use the long i diphthong, as in 'side' or 'tied'. Don't shorten the vowel to 'pid' as in 'pick'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive. It describes coloring, often of animals or birds, and can sound attractive or striking.
nuance.usage_note: Americans mostly meet 'pied' in set expressions and names, such as 'pied wagtail' for a bird or 'the Pied Piper' from the folktale. It is rarely used to describe people or everyday objects. For a horse or cow, Americans more often say 'black and white' or use 'piebald' or 'spotted'.

distinctions.note: Spotted suggests small distinct dots, while pied suggests larger irregular patches of two or more colors.
Piebald usually describes horses with black and white patches, while pied is a more general term for any animal, bird, or object.
Dappled suggests softer, scattered spots of color or light, while pied suggests more distinct patches of contrasting colors.

examples.everyday: Look at that black-and-white cat, the pied one sleeping in the window.
examples.professional: The breeder's catalog lists each rabbit's pied coat pattern so buyers can compare litters.
examples.analytical: The poet's pied landscape of snow and dark pines captures the contrast between the bleak and the bright.

nuance.analogy: Like a Holstein cow, its coat broken into large patches of two contrasting colors.
nuance.etymology: From pie, an old word for magpie, whose black-and-white plumage gave the term its meaning.
common_mistakes: Confusing 'pied' with the dessert 'pie' in speech, since they sound the same.
Using 'pied' for people's clothing or hair; it is mostly used for animals and natural patterns.

pied.etymology: From archaic *pie* (“magpie”), from Old French *pie*, from Latin *pica*.

senses.definition: A cogged (toothed) gear.
A toy for children, comprising an artificial (usually plastic) stem and a flower that spins round in the wind like a tiny windmill.
senses.example: Our daughter spun her pinwheel in the breeze while waiting for the ice cream truck.

senses.definition: A firework that spins in the shape of a spinning wheel.
senses.example: The fireworks show ended with a pinwheel that spun brightly against the dark sky.

senses.definition: A pastry made by laying out dough flat, smearing a topping over it and rolling it up into a spiral, then baking it, resulting in a swirl of filling.
senses.example: For breakfast she baked cinnamon pinwheels with a sweet apple filling.

senses.definition: Any food product consisting of layers (for example of pastry and sweet filling, or of bread and meat) rolled into a spiral.
senses.example: The party platter held turkey pinwheels, rolled tortillas filled with cream cheese and spinach.

senses.definition: To spin.
senses.example: The damaged fighter jet pinwheeled out of control, the g-forces pushing the pilot so hard he couldn't reach the ejection switch.

core.definition: A toy with a stick and colorful paper or plastic blades that spins in the wind. In machinery, it also means a cogged gear wheel.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, PIN, not the second. Don't pronounce the 'wh' with a breathy h; in American speech it is simply a w sound.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive; it evokes childhood, summer, and playgrounds.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use pinwheel mainly for the children's toy you stick in the grass, and it is often sold at fairs, birthday parties, and gift shops. In the US, pinwheel can also name a ground firework that spins, so context matters at a Fourth of July event. In engineering talk, the gear sense is less common.

distinctions.note: A windmill is a large structure that harnesses wind for power or grinding, while a pinwheel is a small toy that spins in a light breeze.
A cog is a single tooth on a gear, while a pinwheel in mechanical use refers to the whole toothed wheel.

collocations: stick a pinwheel in the grass

examples.everyday: The kids ran around the backyard with pinwheels spinning in the breeze.
examples.professional: The old conveyor had a worn pinwheel gear that kept skipping teeth, so we ordered a replacement.
examples.analytical: A pinwheel turns steady moving air into visible rotation, a simple demonstration of how force becomes motion.

nuance.analogy: A tiny windmill you can hold in your hand.
nuance.etymology: Compound of pin and wheel.
common_mistakes: Stressing the second syllable, saying pin-WHEEL.
Adding a breathy h at the start, as in hwheel.

senses.definition: In a placid manner.

core.definition: In a calm, peaceful way, without showing anxiety, anger or agitation.

pronunciation.tip: The first vowel is short, as in cat, not long as in place. Stress the first syllable, and end with a light ee sound.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It suggests calm, steadiness, and an untroubled manner.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use placidly mostly in written descriptions, novels, and reviews. In conversation people normally say 'calmly' or 'peacefully' instead. The word fits well when describing animals, water, or people who stay composed under pressure.

distinctions.note: Calmly is the everyday word for speaking or acting without agitation. Placidly suggests a steady, naturally untroubled temperament.
Serenely has a lofty, almost spiritual tone, often for a sense of inner peace. Placidly is more about a quiet outward manner.
Peacefully describes a quiet situation or a gentle death. Placidly describes a person or creature behaving calmly.

examples.everyday: The cat just lay there placidly while the kids yelled around it.
examples.professional: She listened placidly to the criticism and then asked for specific examples.
examples.analytical: A skeptic like Hume can live placidly in ordinary life while doubting the foundations of knowledge.

nuance.analogy: Placidly is like a lake on a windless morning: smooth on the surface, even when the world around it is busy.
nuance.etymology: From placid, from Latin placidus, 'pleasing, calm', plus the adverb suffix -ly.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing placid with a long a, as in PLAY-sid, instead of a short a.
Confusing placid with placed or with plaid.

senses.definition: A town's public square.
senses.example: Tourists gathered in the central plaza.

senses.definition: An open area used for gathering in a city, often having small trees and sitting benches.
A strip mall.
senses.example: We picked up groceries at the plaza off Route 9, next to the dry cleaner.

senses.definition: A shopping mall.
senses.example: The hotel overlooks a busy shopping plaza.

core.definition: A large open public square in a town or city, often paved, with benches and trees, where people gather.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the first syllable, so say PLAH-zuh, not PLAY-zuh. The final a is a weak schwa, not a long ah sound.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive; it suggests an open, lively public space.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use plaza for a public square in a downtown, or for a hotel or civic space with fountains and benches. In American retail, a shopping plaza is a row of stores with a parking lot, so the word can also mean a strip mall. Context usually makes the meaning clear.

distinctions.note: Square is the general word for an open public space in a town; plaza often suggests a paved, modern or urban space, and it is also used for commercial strips.
A mall is an enclosed building with many stores, while a plaza is usually open-air and may be a single outdoor space or a strip of stores.

examples.everyday: Let's meet by the fountain in the plaza after dinner.
examples.professional: The developer plans to add a small plaza with seating in front of the new office building.
examples.analytical: The city's central plaza functions as a stage for civic life, where political speech and everyday commerce meet.

nuance.analogy: A plaza is like a living room for a whole town, where everyone can gather in the open air.
nuance.etymology: From Spanish plaza, from Latin platea, from Greek plateia, meaning a broad street.
common_mistakes: Saying PLAY-zuh instead of PLAH-zuh.
Using plaza for an indoor shopping center; in American usage it is usually open-air.

plaza.etymology: Spanish *plaza* (“town-square or central place of gathering”), from Latin *platea*, from Ancient Greek *πλατεῖα*, clipping of *πλατεῖα ὁδός* (“broad way”).

senses.definition: The quality or state of being pliable; flexibility; pliableness.

core.definition: The quality of being easy to bend, shape, or influence; flexibility or adaptability.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on BIL. The first syllable is 'ply' as in 'ply' the verb, and the final -ity is 'ih-tee.'

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive. It can praise adaptability, but it can also suggest someone too easily influenced.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use pliability mainly for materials, bodies, or people's attitudes in writing and formal talk. In everyday speech they more often say 'flexibility.' For people, pliability can sound critical, suggesting weakness or being easily swayed.

distinctions.note: Flexibility is the common everyday word for both physical bending and willingness to adjust. Pliability is more formal and emphasizes softness or easy shaping.
Malleability specifically means the ability to be hammered or shaped without breaking, often used for metals. Pliability is broader.

examples.everyday: I like how much pliability this leather jacket has, so it fits comfortably after a few weeks.
examples.professional: We need more pliability in the project schedule so the team can respond to changing requirements.
examples.analytical: Aristotle's ethics assumes a kind of moral pliability in young people, who must be shaped by habit before reason fully takes hold.

nuance.analogy: Pliability is like fresh bread dough: it stretches and takes shape easily, but it can still hold the form you give it.
nuance.etymology: From Late Latin plicabilis, from Latin plicare, 'to fold, bend.'
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the first syllable as 'pleye' rather than 'ply'.
Using pliability for an object that is simply bendy when a more natural word is flexible.

senses.definition: A change in the direction or expected outcome of the plot of a film, novel, or other narrative work.
senses.example: The novel's ending included a shocking plot twist that changed everything the reader believed.

core.definition: A sudden, unexpected change in the direction or outcome of a story, movie, or situation.

pronunciation.tip: Both words are stressed about equally in compound-noun style, but the main stress usually falls on TWIST in the phrase. In fast speech, 'plot' often flaps and the t in 'twist' is soft.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive. It usually signals excitement or surprise, though it can be negative if the twist feels forced.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use plot twist often in conversations about movies, TV shows, and books, and also in real life when something unexpected happens. It is informal and friendly. Someone might say 'plot twist!' ironically after an unexpected event. A natural reply is 'No way!' or 'I didn't see that coming.'

distinctions.note: Surprise is any unexpected event. A plot twist refers specifically to a change in a story or a story-like situation.
A cliffhanger ends an episode in suspense. A plot twist changes the direction of the story.

examples.everyday: Wait, did you see the plot twist at the end? I totally didn't expect that.
examples.professional: The quarterly results were a plot twist, since nobody predicted the customer surge.
examples.analytical: The novel's central plot twist recasts the narrator as the unreliable agent of the crime, forcing readers to reconsider every earlier scene.

nuance.analogy: A plot twist is like a road that suddenly turns when you thought it would go straight: you still arrive somewhere, but not where you expected.
nuance.etymology: Plot comes from Old French complot, 'plan.' Twist comes from Old English and Germanic roots meaning 'to wind or turn.'
common_mistakes: Saying 'plot twists' for a single unexpected change, when the singular is normal in conversation.
Using it for a random surprise in real life without a story-like sense; it is informal.

conversation.text: I didn't see that plot twist coming at all.
The plot twist at the end changes everything.
Plot twist: the restaurant was closed when we got there.

senses.definition: A pronged connecting device which fits into a mating socket, especially an electrical one.
senses.example: I pushed the plug back into the electrical socket and the lamp began to glow again.

senses.definition: An electric socket: wall plug.
senses.example: I plugged the laptop charger into the wall plug beside my desk.

senses.definition: Any piece of wood, metal, or other substance used to stop or fill a hole.
senses.example: Pull the plug out of the tub so it can drain.

senses.definition: A flat oblong cake of cured and pressed tobacco; the tobacco that constitutes it.
senses.example: He preferred a plug to snuff.

senses.definition: A high, tapering silk hat.
senses.example: The old magician tipped his plug hat to the cheering crowd.

senses.definition: A worthless horse.
senses.example: That sorry old plug is ready for the glue factory!

senses.definition: A block of wood let into a wall to afford a hold for nails.
senses.example: The carpenter tapped a wooden plug into the brick wall to hold the shelf bracket.

senses.definition: A promotion (act of promoting) of a product (such as a book, film or play) or other thing, concept, etc, for example during an interview or a commercial.
senses.example: During the interview, the author put in a plug for his latest novel.

senses.definition: A type of lure consisting of a rigid, buoyant or semi-buoyant body and one or more hooks.
senses.example: The fisherman cast the plug into a likely pool, hoping to catch a whopper.

senses.definition: A small seedling grown in a tray from expanded polystyrene or polythene filled usually with a peat or compost substrate.
senses.example: We bought a tray of basil plugs to transplant into the garden beds this spring.

senses.definition: A growth of protoplasm that closes the pore openings in the cells of certain algae.
senses.example: Under the microscope, the algal cells showed a protoplasmic plug sealing each pore opening.

senses.definition: A short cylindrical piece of jewelry commonly worn in larger-gauge body piercings, especially in the ear.
senses.example: She wore a dark wooden plug in her stretched earlobe at the concert.

senses.definition: A drug dealer.
senses.example: Cops arrested the plug outside the apartment complex after a tip from a neighbor.

senses.definition: A trusted connection; someone who provides illicit goods and resources.
senses.example: My cousin always knows who to call; he's got a plug for everything in town.

senses.definition: A branch from a water-pipe to supply a hose.
senses.example: The plumber attached a plug to the outdoor spigot so we could run the garden hose.

senses.definition: A standard, modular fuselage component that can be added or removed.
senses.example: Engineers swapped the cargo plug in the rear fuselage to convert the jet for passengers.

senses.definition: Ellipsis of spark plug.
senses.example: I changed the plugs and the coil packs.

senses.definition: Ellipsis of fireplug (“fire hydrant”).
A body of once molten rock that hardened in a volcanic vent. Usually round or oval in shape.
senses.example: Pressure built beneath the plug in the caldera, eventually resulting in a catastrophic explosion of pyroclastic shrapnel and ash.

senses.definition: (dated) Any worn-out or useless article.
senses.example: Don't keep that useless plug around, it's just a worthless piece of junk now.
senses.label: dated

senses.definition: (dated) A book that fails to sell.
senses.example: The publisher called the novel a plug after it sold fewer than two hundred copies.
senses.label: dated

senses.definition: To stop with a plug; to make tight by stopping a hole.
senses.example: He attempted to plug the leaks with some caulk.

senses.definition: To promote (something, especially a product or service); to mention (something) as if promoting or advertising it.
senses.example: The main guest on the show just kept plugging his latest movie: it got so tiresome.

senses.definition: To persist or continue with something.
senses.example: Keep plugging at the problem until you find a solution.

senses.definition: To shoot (someone) with a bullet.
senses.example: The robber threatened to plug the clerk if he touched the alarm button.

senses.definition: To have sex with; to penetrate sexually.
senses.example: I’d love to plug him with my strap-on.

senses.definition: To ingest a drug rectally.
senses.example: Nurses warned that plugging drugs rectally carries serious risks of infection and injury.

core.definition: A device with metal prongs that fits into an electrical outlet to connect an appliance or cord to the power supply.

pronunciation.tip: Use the short 'u' as in 'bus' and clearly pronounce the final voiced 'g'. Do not add an extra vowel, as in 'plu-gih'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a practical, everyday word with no emotional charge, though as a verb meaning promote it can sound informal or like advertising.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say 'plug' for the prong end of a cord that goes into the wall, and 'outlet' for the wall socket itself. In everyday talk you can say 'the plug is loose' or 'plug it in'. The verb 'to plug' also means to promote something, as in 'The host plugged the new book', which is informal.

distinctions.note: The outlet is the socket in the wall, while the plug is the part on the end of the cord that goes into it.
A stopper closes a bottle or container opening, while a plug fills a hole in a wall, pipe or tub.

examples.everyday: Hey, can you plug the lamp into that outlet by the couch?
examples.professional: Make sure the server's power plug is seated before we restart the rack.
examples.analytical: The metaphor of the plug and socket suggests that technology only works when the right connection is made.

nuance.analogy: A plug and an outlet work like a key and a lock: the shape must match exactly before the power can flow.
nuance.etymology: From Middle Dutch or Low German plugge, meaning stopper.
common_mistakes: Calling the wall socket a 'plug'; Americans usually say 'outlet'.
Saying 'put the plug in the wall' when you mean the plug goes into the outlet; say 'plug it into the outlet'.

plug.etymology: From Dutch *plug*, from Middle Dutch *plugge* (“peg, plug”), from **pluggi*, from **plugi*.

senses.definition: A little mass of lead, or the like, attached to a line, and used by builders, etc. to indicate a vertical direction.
senses.example: The mason hung a plumb from the scaffold to check that the wall rose straight.

senses.definition: The perpendicular direction or position.
senses.example: The carpenter checked the frame, but the post was just slightly out of plumb.

senses.definition: A weight on the end of a long line, used by sailors to determine the depth of water.
senses.example: The sailors dropped the plumb over the side to find out how deep the harbor was.

senses.definition: Truly vertical, as indicated by a plumb line.
senses.example: Make sure the cabinet is plumb before you fasten the hinges to the frame.

senses.definition: Describing an LBW where the batsman is hit on the pads directly in front of their wicket and should be given out.
senses.example: The replay showed the batter was plumb in front, so the umpire's raised finger was correct.

senses.definition: In a vertical direction; perpendicularly.
senses.example: The cliff dropped plumb into the sea, leaving no ledge for the boats to rest on.

senses.definition: Squarely, directly; deeply, completely.
senses.example: It hit him plumb in the middle of his face.

senses.definition: To determine the depth, generally of a liquid; to sound.
senses.example: The crew plumbed the channel every hour to make sure the ship stayed in deep water.

senses.definition: To attach to a water supply and drain.
senses.example: The kitchen sink is now plumbed in / up.

senses.definition: To think about or explore in depth, to get to the bottom of.
senses.example: to plumb the depths of

senses.definition: To use a plumb bob as a measuring or aligning tool.
senses.example: Before pouring the slab, she plumbed each corner with a bob to confirm the forms were level.

senses.definition: To accurately align vertically or horizontally.
senses.example: He plumbed the shelf brackets so the books would not slide toward the window.

senses.definition: To work as a plumber.
senses.example: After dropping out of college, he plumbed for ten years before opening his own shop.

senses.definition: To position vertically above or below.
senses.example: The crew plumbed the steel column directly above the footing before the welders arrived.

senses.definition: (dated) To seal something with lead.
senses.example: The old ironwork was plumbed with molten lead to keep the joints watertight.
senses.label: dated

senses.definition: (rare) To fall or sink like a plummet.
senses.example: The stock plumbed forty percent in a single afternoon after the earnings report came out.
senses.label: rare

core.definition: To investigate or explore a subject deeply, to get to its real meaning or bottom.

pronunciation.tip: Pronounce it as one syllable with a short 'uh' vowel and a silent 'b.' Many learners add a 'b' sound at the end, which Americans do not pronounce.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive; it suggests serious, careful investigation.
nuance.usage_note: In American English 'plumb' as a verb meaning to explore deeply is mostly formal or literary, found in essays, books, and serious discussion. Everyday speakers would more often say 'get to the bottom of' or 'dig into.' The adjective 'plumb,' meaning exactly vertical, is used in construction, and the adverb 'plumb' is common in informal speech like 'plumb crazy.'

distinctions.note: Explore is broad and neutral; plumb suggests reaching the deepest level of something.
Investigate is the common, general word; plumb is more literary and emphasizes depth.

examples.everyday: I can't believe she managed to plumb the depths of that silly rumor, but I don't think it's worth our time.
examples.professional: Our team needs to plumb the causes of the drop in conversion before we change the pricing model.
examples.analytical: The philosopher aims to plumb the meaning of consciousness rather than merely describe its features.

nuance.analogy: To plumb a subject is like dropping a weighted line into deep water to find the bottom.
nuance.etymology: From Latin plumbum, meaning lead, via the weighted line used to measure depth.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the 'b' in 'plumb' because of the spelling.
Using 'plumb' for a shallow or quick look at a topic.

plumb.etymology: From Middle English *plumbe*, *plumme*, from Old French **plombe*, from Latin *plumba*, plural of *plumbum*.

senses.definition: Synonym of plumber's helper.
senses.example: I bought a plumber's friend to clear the clogged kitchen sink before calling anyone.

core.definition: An informal name for a plunger, a rubber suction cup on a handle used to clear clogged drains and toilets.

pronunciation.tip: The possessive 'plumber's' ends in a 'z' sound after the r, and 'friend' is pronounced 'frend' with one syllable. Keep the stress on 'friend', with a lighter stress on 'plum'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and practical. It is a friendly trade nickname, not an insult.
nuance.usage_note: Most Americans simply say 'plunger' for this tool. 'Plumber's friend' or 'plumber's helper' appears on packaging and in hardware stores, and some people use it as a joke. When asking for it, you can say 'Do you have a plunger?' and a helpful clerk will show you the right aisle.

distinctions.note: Plunger is the standard American word for this tool, while plumber's friend is a more informal or branded name for the same object.
A drain snake is a flexible coiled cable for clearing deep clogs, while a plumber's friend uses suction on the surface of the drain.

collocations: a plumber's friend for the toilet

examples.everyday: Grab the plumber's friend from the garage, because the upstairs toilet is clogged again.
examples.professional: Maintenance keeps a plumber's friend in every restroom stall for quick fixes.
examples.analytical: The humble plumber's friend shows how a simple suction device uses air pressure to solve a problem that looks mechanical.

nuance.analogy: A plumber's friend works like a bicycle pump on a stuck valve: a steady push and pull creates the pressure that moves the blockage.
nuance.etymology: A trade nickname combining plumber and friend; the tool is also called a plunger, from the verb plunge.
common_mistakes: Using 'plumber's friend' to mean a plumber, since the phrase names the tool.
Pronouncing 'plumber's' with an extra syllable, as 'PLUM-ber-zez'.

senses.definition: The state or quality of being poisonous.

core.definition: The quality or degree of being poisonous; how strongly something harms living things when swallowed or touched.

pronunciation.tip: The stress is on POY, with the middle and last syllables reduced. The ending -ness is a short 'nus' sound, so do not add an extra vowel.

nuance.connotation: Negative or neutral. It describes a measurable or observed harm, not a judgment about a person.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use poisonousness outside formal writing, textbooks, or safety reports. In science and public health they normally say toxicity or toxicity level. In everyday talk, people say how poisonous something is.

distinctions.note: Toxicity is the usual technical term for how harmful a substance is, often measured in tests, while poisonousness is a more general word for the same quality.
Venom is the poison an animal delivers by bite or sting, while poisonousness can describe any substance or organism that harms when eaten or touched.

examples.everyday: I read a warning about the poisonousness of those berries, so I'm not eating them.
examples.professional: Our lab report measures the poisonousness of each solvent so we can choose a safer one.
examples.analytical: The poisonousness of a substance depends on dose, route of exposure, and the body's ability to process it.

nuance.analogy: Like a warning score on a scale: it measures how much harm something can do, not just whether it can do harm.
nuance.etymology: From poisonous plus the noun suffix -ness, meaning the state or quality of.
common_mistakes: Using poisonousness in casual speech, where how poisonous or how toxic sounds more natural.
Saying poisonosity, a made-up form that Americans do not use; the correct noun is poisonousness.

senses.definition: Of or pertaining to porphyry.
senses.example: The porphyritic rock sample from the quarry contained large crystals in a fine-grained groundmass.

senses.definition: Containing large crystals in a fine mass of material.

core.definition: Describing igneous rock with large crystals embedded in a fine-grained background mass.

pronunciation.tip: The primary stress falls on the third syllable, RIT. The first syllable has a clear r, the second is a reduced schwa, and the ending is -ik. Do not stress the first syllable or stretch the ending into -eat.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and technical. It is used in geology to describe rock texture.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use porphyritic almost only in geology, petrology, and mineralogy. Non-specialists would say the rock has large crystals in a fine grain. You will hear it in museums, field guides, and geology classes.

distinctions.note: Granitic describes a rock with evenly sized crystals, while porphyritic describes a rock with large crystals in a finer background.
Aphanitic describes rock whose grains are too fine to see, while porphyritic has visible large crystals.
Porphyry is the rock itself, while porphyritic is the adjective describing that texture.

examples.everyday: That rock on the trail has big pinkish crystals in it, so the geologist called it porphyritic.
examples.professional: The sample is porphyritic, so the large crystals probably formed before the lava erupted.
examples.analytical: A porphyritic texture records two stages of cooling: slow growth of large crystals followed by rapid solidification of the matrix.

nuance.analogy: A porphyritic rock is like a fruitcake with large raisins in a smooth batter, where the raisins formed first and the batter set later.
nuance.etymology: From porphyry, from Greek porphyrites, meaning purple stone, plus the suffix -itic.
common_mistakes: Using porphyritic as a noun; the noun is porphyry.
Confusing porphyritic with porphyrin, the chemical compound.

senses.definition: A place on the coast at which ships can shelter, or dock to load and unload cargo or passengers.
A town or city containing such a place, a port city.
A sweep rower that primarily rows with an oar on the port side.
senses.example: Each eight has four ports and four starboards.

senses.definition: An opening or doorway in the side of a ship, especially for boarding or loading; an embrasure through which a cannon may be discharged; a porthole.
senses.example: The sailor leaned out of the port to watch the harbor lights drift past.

senses.definition: A narrow opening between other players' bowls or stones wide enough for a delivered bowl or stone to pass through.
senses.example: She threw her stone straight through the port, sitting perfectly on the button.

senses.definition: An opening where a connection (such as with a pipe) is made.
senses.example: Plumbers installed a new port on the boiler so the gauge could be attached.

senses.definition: An opening with a valve seat such that a valve can control the flow of fluid through the opening.
senses.example: When the valve seat wears down, the port no longer seals and fluid leaks through.

senses.definition: A logical or physical construct in and from which data are transferred. Computer port on Wikipedia.Wikipedia.
senses.example: The laptop's USB port failed, so I connected the printer through the network instead.

senses.definition: A female connector of an electronic device, into which a cable's male connector can be inserted.
senses.example: Plug the charger's cable into the port on the back of the monitor.

senses.definition: A number that delimits a connection for specific processes or parts of a network service.
senses.example: The web server listens on port 443 for encrypted traffic from browsers.

senses.definition: Something used to carry a thing, especially a frame for wicks in candle-making.
senses.example: She hung the wicks from the port so they would dry evenly between dippings.

senses.definition: A program that has been adapted, modified, or recoded so that it works on a different platform; the act of this adapting.
senses.example: Gamers can't wait until a port of the title is released on the new system.

senses.definition: A set of files used to build and install a binary executable file from the source code of an application.
senses.example: I compiled the application from its port, which included all the build files.

senses.definition: A type of very sweet fortified wine, mostly dark red, traditionally made in Portugal.
senses.example: We finished dinner with a glass of tawny port and dark chocolate.

senses.definition: A suitcase or schoolbag.
senses.example: Grandpa packed his port with two clean shirts and his old Bible.

senses.definition: The portfolio of a model or artist or investor.
senses.example: Her agency is updating her port with recent photos before the casting season.

senses.definition: The left-hand side of a vessel, including aircraft, when one is facing forward. Used to unambiguously refer to directions relative to the vessel structure, rather than to a person or object on board.
senses.example: The lookout reported a fishing boat approaching from the port side.

senses.definition: A small medical appliance installed beneath the skin, connected to a vein by a catheter, and used to inject drugs or to draw blood samples.
senses.example: The oncologist implanted a port beneath her collarbone for chemotherapy infusions.

senses.definition: The position of a weapon when ported; a rifle position executed by throwing the weapon diagonally across the front of the body, with the right hand grasping the small of the stock and the barrel sloping upward and crossing the point of the left shoulder.
senses.example: The drill sergeant barked for the recruits to bring their rifles to port arms.

senses.definition: To carry, bear, bring, or transport. See porter.
senses.example: Two men ported the wounded soldier across the wet field on a stretcher.

senses.definition: To adapt, modify, or recode to work on a different platform.
To carry or transfer (an existing telephone number) from one service provider to another.
To turn or put to the left or larboard side of a ship; said of the helm.
senses.example: Port your helm!

senses.definition: To dock at a port.

To hold or carry (a weapon) with both hands so that it lies diagonally across the front of the body, with the barrel or similar part near the left shoulder and the right hand grasping the small of the stock; or, to throw (the weapon) into this position on command.
senses.example: Port arms!

senses.definition: To transfer a voucher or subsidy from one jurisdiction to another.
Of or relating to port, the left-hand side of a vessel when facing the bow.
senses.example: on the port side

core.definition: A harbor on the coast where ships shelter, load and unload cargo or passengers, or the town that contains such a harbor.

pronunciation.tip: Pronounce the r clearly; it is not silent as in British English. Avoid the short vowel of 'pot', which has no r.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it describes a practical, factual place with a range of uses.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say 'the port of Seattle' for both the harbor and the city, and 'the port city' for the town. 'Port' also means the left side of a ship, and it is the name of a sweet fortified wine. In technology, a port is a socket or connection on a device, and in business it can mean to move software to a new system.

distinctions.note: A harbor is a sheltered body of water, while a port is a place with facilities for ships to load and unload.
A dock is a structure where a single boat is tied up; a port is a larger area with many docks and terminals.

examples.everyday: We got off the ferry at the port and walked to a coffee shop by the water.
examples.professional: Our shipment cleared customs at the Port of Oakland yesterday, so it should arrive on Friday.
examples.analytical: The city grew rapidly because its port connected inland farms with global trade routes.

nuance.analogy: Like a bus station for ships, where they stop to load and unload.
nuance.etymology: From Old English port, from Latin portus 'harbor, haven'.
common_mistakes: Saying 'at the ship port' or 'in the port' when the ship is docked; Americans say 'in port' for ships.
Confusing 'port' with 'airport' or 'gate' when meaning a transportation hub for planes.

port.etymology: From Old English *port*, borrowed from Latin *portus* (“port, harbour”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European **pértus* (“crossing”).

senses.definition: The quality of being or having potential.
senses.example: filled with potentiality

senses.definition: An instance of potential: any given possibility.
senses.example: any and all potentialities

senses.definition: An inherent capacity for growth or development.
An aptitude amenable to development; capability.
senses.example: Her coach saw real potentiality in the young swimmer and trained her harder each season.

senses.definition: A possibility or capacity to be something, as opposed to an actuality describing what something actually is at present.
senses.example: Philosophers distinguish the potentiality of an acorn to become an oak from its present actuality as a seed.

senses.definition: Quantum potential.
senses.example: In Bohm's interpretation, the potentiality shapes particle motion without ever exerting a classical force.

core.definition: A possibility of future development or ability that is not yet realized; the capacity to become something.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the -al- syllable, so say puh-ten-shee-AL-uh-tee. The middle syllable is usually pronounced with sh, not t plus sh, in American speech.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive; it usually suggests hope or promise, though it can also suggest danger when a risk is described.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use potentiality in academic, philosophical and formal writing, such as discussing a student's potentiality or the risks of a technology. In everyday talk people usually say potential. The plural potentialities is less common but natural in discussion of options or abilities.

distinctions.note: Potential is the everyday word for something that can develop; potentiality is more formal and abstract, often used in philosophy.
A possibility is a particular thing that might happen, while potentiality is the underlying capacity or quality that makes it possible.
Ability is a skill you have now, while potentiality is a capacity that may or may not develop.

examples.everyday: My mom says every kid has a lot of potentiality, but they need someone to believe in them.
examples.professional: We should look at the potentiality of this data set before we commit more budget to the project.
examples.analytical: Aristotle distinguishes between a thing's potentiality and its actuality, which explains how an acorn is an oak in potential.

nuance.analogy: Potentiality is like a seed in a packet: the full plant is inside it, but it has not yet grown.
nuance.etymology: From Late Latin potentialitas, from potentialis, 'possible,' from potens, 'powerful.'
common_mistakes: Using potentiality where potential is the natural everyday word, which can sound stiff.
Pronouncing the middle as tee-ahn instead of ten-shee.
Using it as a countable noun with the wrong plural in everyday speech.

senses.definition: The symbol £, representing the pound sterling.
senses.example: In the London shop, every price tag showed the pound sign in bold black ink.

senses.definition: The symbol # on a telephone.
The symbol #, denoting weight in pounds.
senses.example: A bag of peanuts is marked "5".

core.definition: The # symbol on a telephone keypad or computer keyboard, used in phone menus and as a shortcut key.

pronunciation.tip: In this compound noun, the main stress falls on POUND, and 'sign' is lighter. Do not stress both words equally, and do not say 'sine' with a long i in casual speech.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a practical, everyday term.
nuance.usage_note: In the US, the symbol # is called the pound sign or the pound key, especially in phone menus, where you might hear 'press pound'. The symbol £ is the British pound sign. If you say 'pound sign' in an American store or office, people will assume you mean #. Social media users usually call the same symbol a 'hashtag'.

distinctions.note: Hashtag refers to the # symbol used on social media before a topic word. Pound sign refers to the key or symbol on phones and keyboards.
Number sign is a more formal or technical name for the same symbol. Americans usually say pound sign or pound key in everyday speech.

examples.everyday: Press the pound sign after you enter your PIN, and the call will go through.
examples.professional: The phone menu sends callers to an agent when they press the pound sign, so we need to keep that option visible.
examples.analytical: The name pound sign is often traced to the symbol's old use as an abbreviation for pound, a reminder that symbols can outlive their first meanings.

nuance.analogy: Like a word that means different things on different sides of the ocean, depending on which system you are using.
nuance.etymology: Pound is from Old English pund, from Latin pondo 'by weight'; sign is from Latin signum 'mark'.
common_mistakes: Using 'pound sign' to mean the British £ symbol in an American setting, where people will assume #.
Stressing both words equally instead of putting the main stress on POUND.
Saying 'pound' as 'pond', which changes the vowel sound.

senses.definition: Lacking sufficient power or strength.
senses.example: Stranded without electricity for three days, the hospital felt powerless against the storm.

senses.definition: Lacking legal authority.
senses.example: The traffic warden was powerless to stop me driving away.

senses.definition: Without electricity or electrical power.
senses.example: During the storm, the entire neighborhood was left powerless for several hours

core.definition: Without the strength, authority, or ability to change a situation or protect oneself from something.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on POW, and the final -less is a short unstressed syllable that sounds like 'lis' with a quick vowel. The r in power is pronounced clearly in American English.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It describes a state of helplessness or lack of control, often with a sense of frustration or sadness.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say 'feel powerless' or 'powerless to help' about personal, political, or emotional situations. It is common in news, politics, and everyday talk about bills, bosses, or illness. A natural reply to someone describing a hard situation is 'I know, it's frustrating,' since powerless invites sympathy.

distinctions.note: Helpless means unable to take care of oneself or act without assistance, while powerless means lacking authority or control over the outcome.
Weak describes low physical or structural strength, while powerless describes a lack of authority or capacity to act.

examples.everyday: I felt powerless when the airline canceled our flight and nobody would help us.
examples.professional: Our team feels powerless when budget decisions are made without any input from engineering.
examples.analytical: The essay argues that the poor are often rendered powerless not by weakness but by institutions that deny them a voice.

nuance.analogy: Like a phone with a dead battery: the device is still there, but it cannot do anything.
nuance.etymology: From power with the suffix -less, meaning without power.
common_mistakes: Using 'powerless of' instead of 'powerless to' or 'powerless against'.
Confusing powerless with weak when speaking about physical strength.

senses.definition: The study of the use of language, especially meaning, in a social context; it includes extratextual aspects of language including exophoric reference, phatic utterances, and nonverbal channels.

core.definition: The branch of linguistics studying how context and speaker intention shape what an utterance means beyond its literal words.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on MAT, and the final syllable is an unstressed 'iks' ending in an s sound, not z. Learners often split the middle into separate syllables, as in prag-ma-tics.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and technical.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use pragmatics mainly in linguistics, philosophy and language-technology work, such as chatbot design. In everyday talk, do not use it to mean practical behavior; say practicality or a practical approach. It names a field of study and is usually treated as a singular noun.

distinctions.note: Semantics studies the literal meaning of words and sentences; pragmatics studies how context and intention change what is meant.
Syntax concerns sentence structure and word order, while pragmatics concerns language use in context.

examples.everyday: My linguistics professor says that 'Can you pass the salt?' is really a request, which is why pragmatics fascinates me.
examples.professional: For the chatbot evaluation, we need to test pragmatics, such as whether it catches sarcasm or polite requests, not just grammar.
examples.analytical: Pragmatics shows that a speaker's meaning often depends on shared assumptions, so literal sentences can carry unstated implications.

nuance.analogy: If semantics is the dictionary definition of each word, pragmatics is the meaning you get from how someone says it.
nuance.etymology: From Greek pragmatikos, 'of business or action', from pragma, 'deed or thing done'.
common_mistakes: Confusing pragmatics the field with pragmatic, the everyday word for practical.
Stressing the wrong syllable, as prag-MA-tics.

senses.definition: Secondhand.
senses.example: She bought a pre-owned Subaru with low mileage from a dealership in Denver.

core.definition: Previously owned by someone else; used, and usually sold as used by a dealer or seller.

pronunciation.tip: The primary stress falls on owned, and pre has a light secondary stress. Pre is pronounced like 'pree', with a clear long e, and owned has the long o diphthong.

nuance.connotation: Positive or polite. It is a softer, more respectable term than 'used', often used in advertising.
nuance.usage_note: 'Pre-owned' is standard in car dealerships and luxury goods sales, especially 'certified pre-owned' vehicles. Many Americans say 'used' or 'secondhand' in everyday talk, and some find 'pre-owned' a bit like marketing language. The hyphen is standard, though 'preowned' also appears.

distinctions.note: Used is plain and direct and is the everyday word in American conversation; pre-owned sounds more polished and commercial.
Secondhand is casual and often describes goods bought from individuals or thrift stores; pre-owned is common in dealer and retail contexts.
Refurbished means repaired or restored to working order; pre-owned only means previously owned, with no guarantee of repair.

examples.everyday: We bought a pre-owned Honda from a dealer down the street, and it's been great for the commute.
examples.professional: Our pre-owned inventory sold faster than the new models this quarter, so we are ordering more trade-ins.
examples.analytical: Calling a used car pre-owned signals respectability, but the label does not change the vehicle's history or wear.

nuance.analogy: Pre-owned is like a well-tailored suit from a previous season: the same garment, presented in a way that feels more respectable.
nuance.etymology: Pre- from Latin prae, before; owned from Old English agen, own.
common_mistakes: Dropping the hyphen or writing it as one word inconsistently in formal writing.
Stressing pre, as in 'PREE-owned', rather than owned.

senses.definition: Occurring before or in preparation for dinner.

core.definition: Happening before dinner, or done in preparation for dinner, such as drinks, snacks or a short walk.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the first syllable, PREE, and the final -er is a reduced, r-colored vowel that sounds like ur. The middle vowel is short, as in the word din.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and pleasant. It suggests relaxed hospitality before a meal.
nuance.usage_note: Americans most often use this word for hosting, cocktails and restaurants, as in pre-dinner drinks. Most American writers hyphenate it as pre-dinner, and many simply say before dinner in speech. It is a casual, friendly word, not a stiff one.

distinctions.note: Before-dinner is more common in spoken American English and is often used as a compound adjective, while predinner is more compact and often appears in writing.
An appetizer is a specific food served to start a meal, while predinner describes the time or activity that comes before dinner.

examples.everyday: We had a few pre-dinner drinks on the porch before the kids got hungry.
examples.professional: The pre-dinner briefing will cover the schedule for tomorrow's client visit, so please arrive a few minutes early.
examples.analytical: Pre-dinner conversation in a host's home often reveals the social expectations that the formal meal will later enforce.

nuance.analogy: Like the warm-up before a game, which prepares you for the main event.
nuance.etymology: From pre- meaning before, and dinner, from Old French disner, to eat the first meal of the day.
common_mistakes: Spelling it as two separate words, pre dinner, in formal writing.
Using predinner for a food item; it describes timing or purpose, while appetizer names the dish.
Stressing the second syllable instead of the first.

senses.definition: (obsolete) To warn of something in advance.
senses.label: obsolete

core.definition: (archaic) To warn someone of something beforehand. Americans today use 'warn in advance' or 'forewarn' instead.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the second syllable, MAH. The -ish ending is a short 'ish' sound, as in 'finish'. The first vowel is a reduced 'ih'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it sounds old and formal, which can make it seem stiff or pretentious in modern speech.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use 'premonish' today. You may find it in older sermons, 17th-century writing, or historical novels, and modern dictionaries mark it as obsolete. In everyday English, say 'warn someone ahead of time' or 'forewarn someone'.

distinctions.note: 'Forewarn' is still used in modern English, especially in writing, while 'premonish' is obsolete and sounds archaic.
A 'premonition' is a feeling or sense that something bad will happen, while 'premonish' is an act of warning someone.

examples.everyday: I found the word premonish in an old church bulletin, and I had to look it up because nobody says it anymore.
examples.professional: The style guide flags premonish as obsolete, so in the report please use warn in advance instead.
examples.analytical: The seventeenth-century preacher premonished his congregation of divine judgment, using a vocabulary that modern readers no longer share.

nuance.analogy: Like a road sign for a bridge that was demolished long ago, the word still points to a meaning, but nobody travels that way anymore.
nuance.etymology: From Latin praemonere 'to warn beforehand', from prae 'before' and monere 'to warn'.
common_mistakes: Using it in modern writing, where it will sound archaic or wrong.
Confusing the verb 'premonish' with the noun 'premonition'.
Putting the stress on the first syllable instead of the second.

senses.definition: The proposition that nothing happens without a sufficient reason why it should be as it is and not otherwise.
senses.example: Leibniz's principle of sufficient reason shaped my seminar paper on divine creation.

core.definition: The philosophical principle that everything that exists or happens has a sufficient reason or cause explaining why it is as it is.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on FISH in 'sufficient' and on REE in 'reason', so do not stress the second syllable of 'sufficient'. 'Of' is reduced to 'uhv', and the r in 'reason' should be American and rhotic.

nuance.connotation: Neutral: it is a technical philosophical term with no emotional charge.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this phrase in philosophy courses, metaphysics discussions and academic writing, especially when discussing Leibniz. It is rarely used in everyday talk. A natural reply in a seminar is to ask for the principle's formulation or its implications.

distinctions.note: Causality says every event has a cause, while the principle of sufficient reason is broader and asks for an explanation, which can be causal or logical.
Non-contradiction is about what can be true or false together, while sufficient reason concerns why things exist or happen as they do.

collocations: invoke the principle of sufficient reason
reject the principle of sufficient reason

examples.everyday: My roommate asked why the sky is blue, and I joked that it's basically the principle of sufficient reason, since there has to be an explanation.
examples.professional: In the design review, our lead engineer said we should not accept an unexplained model output, because the principle of sufficient reason requires a reason for every result.
examples.analytical: Leibniz used the principle of sufficient reason to argue that the world must have a sufficient reason for being as it is, which he took to point toward God.

nuance.analogy: It is like a detective who refuses to accept that a clue appeared for no reason and insists that every fact must have an explanation.
nuance.etymology: From Latin principium, beginning or first principle, and sufficiens, enough; systematized by Leibniz in the early eighteenth century.
common_mistakes: Stressing 'sufficient' on the second syllable, saying 'suh-FISH-ent' with an extra vowel in the middle.
Using 'reason' to mean a personal motive only, when the principle concerns any explanation for existence or fact.

senses.definition: Synonym of inside joke (“a joke that is understood or meant to be understood only by certain people who are aware of the details”).
senses.example: Nobody else laughed, since the private joke only made sense to the two of us.

core.definition: A joke understood only by a small group who share the context or history behind it.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on JOKE, not on PRIV-. The long o is a true diphthong, so say 'johk', not 'jock'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive when it signals friendship, but it can make outsiders feel left out.
nuance.usage_note: Friends, couples and coworkers often share private jokes based on past events. When someone else laughs and you do not, people say 'Sorry, it's a private joke,' and a natural reply is 'Oh, you had to be there,' or simply 'Ha, got it.' The term is informal and friendly.

distinctions.note: A running joke is repeated over time and often develops variations, while a private joke can be a single reference understood by a few people.
The two are nearly interchangeable, but 'inside joke' is more common in everyday American speech.

examples.everyday: Sorry, that was a private joke between Sam and me.
examples.professional: Our team has a private joke about the two-week sprint, so new hires may miss the reference.
examples.analytical: A private joke can build solidarity while quietly marking outsiders as not belonging to the group.

nuance.analogy: A private joke is like a key that opens only one door in a house: everyone can see the door, but only a few can go through it.
nuance.etymology: Private from Latin privatus ('set apart'); joke from Latin iocus ('jest').
common_mistakes: Saying 'a private joke with me' instead of 'a private joke between us'.
Pronouncing 'joke' with a short vowel, like 'jock'.

senses.definition: A political ideology that favours progress towards better conditions in society.

core.definition: A political ideology favoring social reform, government action to improve conditions, and progress toward a more just society.

pronunciation.tip: The stress is on GRESS, and the -ism ending is a short, unstressed syllable, so it sounds like -iz-um. Don't stress the final syllable.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to politically charged. Supporters see it positively; opponents may use it critically, so tone depends on who is speaking.
nuance.usage_note: In the United States, Progressivism usually refers to the reform movement of roughly 1890 to 1920, which fought trusts, corruption, and unsafe working conditions, and also to later liberal policy positions. Americans capitalize it when naming the historical movement, as in 'the Progressive Era.' Avoid using it casually in everyday talk, since it can signal a political stance that people may hear as partisan.

distinctions.note: Liberalism is a broader tradition centered on individual rights and liberty; progressivism emphasizes active government reform and social improvement.
Progressiveness is a quality of mind or attitude; progressivism is a named ideology with a history and program.

examples.everyday: My uncle always talks about the Progressive Era when we discuss why cities started building parks, so I learned a lot from him.
examples.professional: Our policy brief summarizes how Progressivism shaped the early regulation of food safety in the United States.
examples.analytical: Historians argue that American progressivism combined faith in expert administration with a moral vision of a more equitable public life.

nuance.analogy: Like a gardener who keeps pruning and planting, always working to improve the garden rather than leaving it as it is.
nuance.etymology: From progressive plus -ism, from Latin progressus, a going forward.
common_mistakes: Using lowercase progressivism for the historical movement; Americans usually capitalize the Progressive Era.
Using progressivism as a synonym for any new idea, when it refers specifically to a political and reform movement.

senses.definition: To use or spread propaganda.
To tell propaganda to someone in an attempt to influence one's views.
senses.example: The state broadcaster began to propagandize schoolchildren with daily lessons about the glorious harvest.

senses.definition: To use something or someone in propaganda purposes.

core.definition: To spread propaganda, or to try to win people over to a cause with one-sided messages.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on 'gan.' The ending '-ize' is pronounced /aɪz/, like 'eyes,' not like the 'eez' of 'freeze' or the 'dize' of 'dizzy.'

nuance.connotation: Negative. It implies manipulation or one-sided messaging.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'propagandize' in political, historical, and media criticism, for example when a government or group repeatedly pushes one message. It is less common in casual speech, where people say 'push their agenda' or 'spin the story.' The verb is often followed by 'for' or 'against' with a cause or group.

distinctions.note: Indoctrinate means to teach beliefs uncritically, often over a long time, while propagandize focuses on repeated messaging.
Persuade is neutral and can describe honest argument, while propagandize implies one-sided manipulation.
Promote is neutral and can describe ordinary advertising or advocacy, while propagandize carries a negative charge.

examples.everyday: My cousin's favorite cable channel constantly propagandizes its viewers, so I've stopped watching it.
examples.professional: We shouldn't let the vendor propagandize the results; let's show the raw numbers and let people judge.
examples.analytical: Totalitarian regimes often propagandize their citizens by controlling schools, newspapers, and public ceremonies.

nuance.analogy: Like a commercial that repeats one slogan until it sounds like the only possible truth.
nuance.etymology: From 'propaganda' plus the verb suffix '-ize.'
common_mistakes: Dropping 'for' or 'against' when the object is a cause, as in 'propagandize for the cause.'
Confusing 'propagandize' with 'propagate,' which means to spread or reproduce something.

senses.definition: The arch that frames a theater stage, and separates it from the auditorium.

core.definition: The arch that frames a theater stage and separates the stage from the auditorium, where the audience sits.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on SEE in proscenium, and the s is a plain s sound, not sh. The word arch is stressed in the phrase, so say ARCH clearly at the end.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a precise theater term and carries no emotional tone.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use proscenium arch mainly in theater, architecture and design talk. In casual conversation people say 'the stage' or 'the frame of the stage' instead. You might hear it when someone describes a theater seating chart or a show that is staged in a traditional way.

distinctions.note: Stage is the whole performance area, while proscenium arch is the frame at its front edge that separates the stage from the audience.
The apron is the part of the stage that extends in front of the proscenium arch toward the audience.

collocations: the height of the proscenium arch

examples.everyday: We had seats right up near the proscenium arch at the old theater downtown, so the view was great.
examples.professional: The lighting designer needs to adjust the rigging so the set fits within the proscenium arch for the touring show.
examples.analytical: The proscenium arch creates a frame that separates the fictional world of the play from the audience's real space.

nuance.analogy: Like a picture frame around a painting, marking where the artwork begins and ends.
nuance.etymology: From Greek proskēnion, from pro 'in front of' and skēnē 'stage building' or 'tent'.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing proscenium with a sh sound, as in PRO-shen-ee-um.
Placing the stress on the first syllable as PRO-sen-ee-um, which sounds unnatural in American speech.

senses.definition: The first leaf of a roll of papyrus, or the official mark typically found on such a page.
senses.example: The scribe's name appeared on the protocol, the first leaf of the papyrus roll.

senses.definition: The official formulas which appeared at the beginning or end of certain official documents such as charters, papal bulls etc.
senses.example: The medieval charter opened with a protocol that named the king and invoked divine authority.

senses.definition: The original notes of observations made during an experiment.
senses.example: She recorded every observation in the protocol, noting temperatures and timestamps before analyzing any results.

senses.definition: The precise method for carrying out or reproducing a given experiment.
senses.example: Follow the protocol exactly so that another lab can reproduce the trial results.

senses.definition: The official rules and guidelines for heads of state and other dignitaries, governing accepted behavior in relations with other diplomatic representatives or over affairs of state.
senses.example: The ambassador reminded the visiting delegation that protocol required a formal greeting at the airport.

senses.definition: An accepted code of conduct; acceptable behavior in a given situation or group.
senses.example: At a funeral, it is simply protocol to speak quietly and dress conservatively.

senses.definition: A set of formal rules describing how to transmit or exchange data, especially across a network.
senses.example: The browser and server negotiate a secure connection using the HTTPS protocol before any data moves.

senses.definition: The introduction of a liturgical preface, immediately following the Sursum corda dialogue.
senses.example: After the Sursum corda, the priest chanted the protocol that introduces the preface.

senses.definition: In some programming languages, a data type declaring a set of members that must be implemented by a class or other data type.
senses.example: The interface protocol requires every class that implements it to define a serialize method.

senses.definition: An amendment to an official treaty.
senses.example: The senators approved a protocol to the treaty that extended the deadline for arms inspections.

senses.definition: The set of instructions allowing a licensed medical professional to start, modify, or stop a medical or patient care order.
senses.example: The nurse called the physician to confirm the protocol before adjusting the patient's insulin dose.

senses.definition: (historical) The minutes, or official record, of a negotiation or transaction; especially a document drawn up officially which forms the legal basis for subsequent agreements based on it.
senses.example: The clerk recorded the protocol of the negotiation, which later served as the basis for the contract.
senses.label: historical

senses.definition: (rare) An official record of a diplomatic meeting or negotiation; later specifically, a draft document setting out agreements to be signed into force by a subsequent formal treaty.
